With \(g = f + f''\) we get \(\nabla^4\varphi = (f + 2f'' + f'''')/r^3\).
  3. The equation \(f'''' + 2f'' + f = 0\) has the characteristic polynomial \((s^2 + 1)^2\) with the double roots \(\pm\mathrm{i}\). By theorem 9.39 every solution has the form \((p + q\theta)\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta} + (\bar p + \bar q\theta)\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}\) and by corollary 9.40 the real solutions are the linear combinations of \(\cos\theta\), \(\sin\theta\), \(\theta\cos\theta\), \(\theta\sin\theta\). For \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) we have \(f + f'' = 0\). For \(\theta\cos\theta\), \(f'' = -2\sin\theta - \theta\cos\theta\), so \(f + f'' = -2\sin\theta\), for \(\theta\sin\theta\), \(f'' = 2\cos\theta - \theta\sin\theta\) and \(f + f'' = 2\cos\theta\). With claim 1 the expression for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) follows.

Source: SADD (8.4.31)-(8.4.32) (PDF p. 199-200) and BARBER (12.2)-(12.3) (PDF p. 186) take from the general Michell solution the terms with the stress \(1/r\). The proof is ours.

The lemma says something surprising: with this form \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) are zero for every \(f\). The stress has only a radial component, so the solution is called the simple radial distribution (BARBER PDF p. 187). The surface is the line \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), its normal is \(\pm\boldsymbol e_\theta\), and the stress vector on it is \(\pm(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta}\boldsymbol e_\theta) = \boldsymbol 0\), so the surface is free by itself. What remains is the force: \(C_3\) gives a stress \(\propto \sin\theta\), which is odd in \(\theta\) and would give the horizontal force \(-\pi C_3\) (03-check.py, C3), while condition 3 of the definition requires a vertical force, so \(C_3 = 0\). The terms with \(C_1\), \(C_2\) give \(\varphi = C_1\,r\cos\theta + C_2\,r\sin\theta = C_1 y + C_2 x\), which is linear and has all stresses zero.

Theorem 25.13 The Flamant solution (Flamantova rešitev)

Let the half-plane \(y > 0\) be as in definition 25.11 and \(F' > 0\). The function \(\varphi = -\dfrac{F'}{\pi}\,r\theta\sin\theta\) (\(r\) and \(\theta\) as in figure 25.9) is biharmonic and its stresses are the stress field of the line force \(F'\). More precisely:

  1. \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -\dfrac{2F'\cos\theta}{\pi r}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\). In Cartesian components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\dfrac{2F'\,y^3}{\pi\,(x^2 + y^2)^2}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\dfrac{2F'\,x^2 y}{\pi\,(x^2 + y^2)^2}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\dfrac{2F'\,x y^2}{\pi\,(x^2 + y^2)^2}\).
  2. The surface is free outside \(O\), and on every half circle \(r = a\) the resultant of the stresses equals \((0, -F')\).
  3. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is constant, \(-2F'/(\pi d)\), on the circle \(r = d\cos\theta\) that touches the surface in \(O\), with diameter \(d\).
  4. Under the force (\(x = 0\)), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2F'/(\pi y)\), and on the line at depth \(a\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}(x)/\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}(0) = (1 + x^2/a^2)^{-2}\).
Proof

We must show that \(\varphi\) satisfies lemma 25.12 with a determined \(C_4\) and that the claims follow.

  1. We take \(f = C_4\,\theta\sin\theta\), so \(f'''' + 2f'' + f = 0\) by lemma 25.12, claim 3, and \(\varphi\) is biharmonic. By claim 1 of the lemma \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) and by claim 3 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 2C_4\cos\theta/r\). By theorem 11.36, claims 1 and 3 (without body force, \(V = 0\), \(\varphi\) has continuous derivatives up to the fourth order on \(y > 0\), where \(r > 0\)), the stresses satisfy equilibrium and the compatibility condition. This is the first condition of definition 25.11.
  2. The arc \(r = a\) has the outer normal \(\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}} = (\sin\theta, \cos\theta)\) in the components \(x\), \(y\) and the force per unit length of arc \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\,\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}}\), since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\). The arc between the angles \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) has length \(a(\theta_2 - \theta_1)\), so the resultant over the arc is an integral over the angle with the factor \(a\), \(\big(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin\theta\,a\,\mathrm{d}\theta,\ \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\cos\theta\,a\,\mathrm{d}\theta\big)\). With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 2C_4\cos\theta/r\) the first component is zero, since the integrand is odd, and the second is \(2C_4\int\cos^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \pi C_4\). The requirement \(\pi C_4 = -F'\) gives \(C_4 = -F'/\pi\), and with it \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -2F'\cos\theta/(\pi r)\). This is the first part of claim 1 and the third condition of the definition.
  3. The surface at \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\): in Cartesian components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\cos^2\theta\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin\theta\cos\theta\) (transformation of stress, theorem 2.42, since \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) are zero). At \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) has the factor \(\cos\theta = 0\) and \(\cos^2\theta = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero at \(r > 0\). This is the second condition of the definition and the first part of claim 2.
  4. Since \(x = r\sin\theta\) and \(y = r\cos\theta\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2F'\cos^3\theta/(\pi r) = -2F'y^3/(\pi r^4)\) and likewise \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin^2\theta\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). This is the rest of claim 1 (checked in SymPy, num-03.py, S4).
  5. On the circle \(r = d\cos\theta\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -2F'\cos\theta/(\pi d\cos\theta) = -2F'/(\pi d)\), claim 3. At \(x = 0\), \(r = y\) and \(\theta = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2F'/(\pi y)\). At \(y = a\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}(x) = -\dfrac{2F'}{\pi a}\,\dfrac{1}{(1 + x^2/a^2)^2}\), claim 4.

Source: SADD §8.4.7, (8.4.34)-(8.4.36) (PDF p. 199-201): the same stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}} = -2Y\sin\theta/(\pi r)\) with the angle measured from the surface (crop 8.4.35 read), and "lines of constant radial stress are circles tangent to the surface" (PDF p. 201). BARBER §12.2-12.3, (12.2)-(12.7), (12.11) (PDF p. 186-188). Neither source discusses uniqueness on the pages cited, see the text below the theorem.

The proof showed that the stress of the theorem satisfies all three conditions of the definition. What does it say? Figure 25.10 shows two panels.

In the left panel there is the surface with the force \(F'\) in \(O\). Through the point \(O\) we draw three circles, all touching the surface in \(O\), with a vertical diameter \(d = 1\), \(2\), \(4\) mm. By claim 3 the stress on each is constant, and the values are \(63{,}66\), \(31{,}83\) and \(15{,}92\) MPa in compression: half for a twice larger diameter. This is the same law \(\sigma \propto 1/r\) as in the motivation. The right panel shows the profile of the stress on the line at depth \(a\): it is largest under the force, at \(x = a\) it is \(\tfrac14\), at \(x = 2a\) only \(0{,}04\) and at \(x = 5a\) only \(0{,}0015\) of the largest value (SymPy and NumPy, num-03.py, N7). The vertical stress on this line is thus gathered under the force, in a strip a few \(a\) wide. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) itself, however, falls only like \(1/r\) (claim 1): at the point \(x = 5a\), \(y = a\) it is still \(1/26 = 0{,}038\) of the value under the force at depth \(a\), only there it points almost horizontally, so its vertical part is small (03-check.py, C5).

Under the force. The compressive stress \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}| = 2F'/(\pi y)\) is \(63{,}7\) MPa at \(y = 1\) mm, \(636{,}6\) MPa at \(0{,}1\) mm and \(6366\) MPa at \(0{,}01\) mm (num-03.py, N2). It goes beyond every bound as \(y \to 0\). This is not a fault of the solution but a measure of the model: a force on a line means a force on zero area. The linear theory assumes that all derivatives of the displacements are below about \(0{,}001\) in size (section 3.2.1, assumption 4). Under the force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero, so by Hooke's law of plane strain (theorem 11.31) the derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/E^*\). The bound \(0{,}001\) at \(E^* = 215{,}4\) GPa thus means a stress of at most \(215{,}4\) MPa, and at \(F' = 100\) N/mm this holds for \(y \geq 2F'/(\pi\cdot 215{,}4\ \mathrm{MPa}) = 0{,}30\) mm. Closer than that the solution does not hold. What a real contact does we see in section 25.5: the force spreads over a strip of finite width.

Is the solution the only one? We proved that the field is a solution, not that it is the only one. By definition 25.11 it is not the only one either. Take the uniform stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = s\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) with any number \(s\). Its Airy function \(s\,y^2/2\) is biharmonic, so it satisfies equilibrium and compatibility. It leaves the surface free, since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero. On the half-disc it gives the force \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} s\sin\theta\,a\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 0\) in the direction \(x\) and zero in the direction \(y\) (03-check.py, C2). Added to Flamant's, it gives another field that satisfies all three conditions of the definition. It is the stress of a horizontal tension or compression at infinity, not a consequence of the force in \(O\). The uniqueness theorem of the boundary value problem (theorem 11.4) holds for bounded bodies and regular data, and a half-plane with a point force is neither, so we cannot use it here, and we do not prove uniqueness under extra conditions at infinity. We proved only this much: among the functions of the form \(r f(\theta)\) only this one gives the stress field of a line force (lemma 25.12 and the paragraph after it).

The displacements follow from the stresses through Hooke's law and the relation between displacements and strains.

Lemma 25.14 Displacements of the Flamant solution (pomiki pri Flamantovi rešitvi)

Let the stress field be that of theorem 25.13 and \(E^*\), \(\nu^*\) as above. The displacement field in local components

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{r}} &= -\frac{F'}{\pi E^*}\Big(2\cos\theta\,\ln r + (1 - \nu^*)\,\theta\sin\theta\Big) , \\ u_\theta &= \frac{F'}{\pi E^*}\Big(2\sin\theta\,\ln r - (1 - \nu^*)\,\theta\cos\theta + (1 + \nu^*)\sin\theta\Big) \end{aligned} \tag{25.10}\]

has strains that by Hooke's law of plane strain give the stresses of theorem 25.13. Every other displacement field with the same strains differs from it by a rigid displacement \((A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta,\ -A\sin\theta + B\cos\theta + W r)\) with constants \(A\), \(B\), \(W\). The field (25.10) has \(u_\theta = 0\) on the line of the force \(\theta = 0\). On the surface (\(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), \(r = |x|\)) it has:

  1. the horizontal displacement of size \(\dfrac{(1 - \nu^*)F'}{2E^*}\) toward \(O\), \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{(1 - \nu^*)F'}{2E^*}\), equal at all \(r\),
  2. the vertical displacement (into the body) \(w(x) = -\dfrac{F'}{\pi E^*}\big(2\ln|x| + 1 + \nu^*\big)\),
  3. the difference of displacements \(w(x_1) - w(x_2) = \dfrac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\ln\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}\) does not depend on the rigid displacement.
Proof

We must show that (25.10) gives the right strains, that it is the only form, and claims 1 to 3. We get the strains in cylindrical coordinates from corollary 11.21 and the stresses from corollary 11.26.

  1. By theorem 11.31 plane strain has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu^*\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E^*\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (\sigma_{\theta\theta} - \nu^*\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})/E^*\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = (1 + \nu^*)\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}/E^*\). With \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}/E^* = -2F'\cos\theta/(\pi E^* r)\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = -\nu^*\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}/E^* = 2\nu^* F'\cos\theta/(\pi E^* r)\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\).
  2. From \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}}\) it follows that \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{2F'\cos\theta}{\pi E^*}\ln r + f(\theta)\) with a so far unknown function \(f\). From \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (u_{\mathrm{r}} + \partial u_\theta/\partial\theta)/r\) it follows that \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = 2\nu^*F'\cos\theta/(\pi E^*) - u_{\mathrm{r}}\). With an integral over \(\theta\), where \(\Phi(\theta)\) is a primitive function of \(f\), \(u_\theta = \dfrac{2F'\sin\theta}{\pi E^*}\big(\ln r + \nu^*\big) - \Phi(\theta) + g(r)\) with an unknown function \(g\).
  3. We multiply the condition \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) by \(2r\) using corollary 11.21 and insert: \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial\theta + r\,\partial u_\theta/\partial r - u_\theta = 0\). The terms with \(\ln r\) cancel and what remains is \(f' + \Phi + c\sin\theta + (r g' - g) = 0\) with \(c = 2(1 - \nu^*)F'/(\pi E^*)\). The first three terms depend only on \(\theta\), the last only on \(r\), so each is constant: \(r g' - g = -K\), \(g = K + W r\), and \(f' + \Phi + c\sin\theta = K\).
  4. The derivative of the last equation with respect to \(\theta\) gives \(f'' + f = -c\cos\theta\). The function \(-\tfrac{c}{2}\,\theta\sin\theta\) solves it, since \((\theta\sin\theta)'' + \theta\sin\theta = 2\cos\theta\). The difference of two solutions solves \(h'' + h = 0\), so by theorem 9.39 it is \(A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta\). Hence \(f = -\tfrac c2\,\theta\sin\theta + A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta\), and from \(f' + \Phi + c\sin\theta = K\) follows \(\Phi\), which agrees with \(f\) (\(\Phi' = f\) is checked by differentiation). Inserted in step 2, \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(u_\theta\) are as (25.10), only with the terms \(A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta\) in \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(-A\sin\theta + B\cos\theta + Wr\) in \(u_\theta\). These terms are a rigid displacement: a shift \((B, A)\) in the directions \(x\), \(y\) and a rotation \(W\) (their strains are zero, SymPy, S9). For (25.10), \(A = B = W = 0\) and \(K\) is already included. Since \(\sin 0 = 0\), \(u_\theta = 0\) at \(\theta = 0\).
  5. On the surface \(\cos\theta = 0\), \(\sin\theta = \pm1\), \(\theta\sin\theta = \pi/2\) and \(\theta\cos\theta = 0\). Hence \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{(1 - \nu^*)F'}{2E^*}\) on both sides. The basis vector \(\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}}\) points along the surface away from \(O\), so the displacement is toward \(O\), and nothing depends on \(r\). This is claim 1.
  6. At \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), \(\boldsymbol e_\theta = (0, \mp1)\) in the components \(x\), \(y\) and \(u_\theta = \pm\dfrac{F'}{\pi E^*}(2\ln r + 1 + \nu^*)\), so the vertical displacement is \(-\dfrac{F'}{\pi E^*}(2\ln r + 1 + \nu^*)\) on both sides. This is claim 2, its difference is claim 3, since the rigid displacement cancels in the difference.

Source: SADD (8.4.37)-(8.4.43) (PDF p. 201-203), crop (8.4.43) read: the same expressions with the angle measured from the surface and for plane stress (\(E\), \(\nu\) in place of \(E^*\), \(\nu^*\) by corollary 11.34). SADD (8.4.44), (8.4.45) (PDF p. 203): all points of the surface move horizontally the same amount toward the force, "an unexpected result". BARBER (12.12), (12.13) (PDF p. 188) the same expression in other notation. We checked the result in SymPy (num-03.py, S6 to S9).

The proof showed that the displacement field is unique up to a rigid displacement and has a simple form on the surface. Figure 25.11 shows it.

In the left panel there is the surface with the force \(F'\), and below it a grid of points, in each a displacement is drawn (\(0{,}28\) cm per unit). Near the force the displacements point down, and along the surface all are equal horizontally and point toward the force, in agreement with claim 1. The points at \(|x| = 2{,}5\) cm, however, rise. This is not a property of the body but of the choice of the rigid displacement, for which the vertical displacement of the surface is zero at \(|x| = 1{,}96\) cm (03-check.py, C6). The right panel shows the surface after deformation: as \(x \to 0\) the sinking goes beyond every bound, like \(\ln(1/|x|)\). The solid line is \(w\) for the choice of the rigid displacement that gives \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -(1 + \nu^*)F'/(\pi E^*)\) at \(|x| = 4\) cm, the dashed one at \(|x| = 40\) cm. They are the same curve, shifted by \(2\ln 10 = 4{,}605\) units of \(F'/(\pi E^*)\), which is \(0{,}68\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) at \(F' = 100\) N/mm.

The sinking is determined only up to a constant. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm, \(2F'/(\pi E^*) = 0{,}2956\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) (num-03.py, N5). The difference of sinking between \(x_1 = 1\) mm and \(x_2 = 10\), \(100\), \(1000\) mm is \(0{,}681\), \(1{,}361\) and \(2{,}042\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) (N6): each tenfold distance adds the same. As \(x_2 \to \infty\) the difference goes beyond every bound, so the displacement \(w\) is never determined at a point but always only relative to a chosen reference point, and this choice is a decision of the model, not a result. The same cause lies behind the stress \(\propto 1/r\): a displacement is an integral of the strain, and \(\int\frac{1}{r}\,\mathrm{d}r = \ln r\) does not converge at infinity (by SADD PDF p. 203 this follows from the radial stress being \(O(1/r)\) and is a feature of the plane model, the three-dimensional solution of section 25.4 has no logarithm). Some authors remove the logarithm with the condition that the point on the load line at a chosen depth \(r_0\) does not move, in our notation \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(r_0, 0) = 0\) (SADD PDF p. 204 writes \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(r_0, \pi/2) = 0\), since it measures the angle from the surface). Then \(\ln(r/r_0)\) stands everywhere in (25.10) in place of \(\ln r\), which is exactly this choice.

Consequence for contact: we do not know the approach. When in section 25.5 two cylinders are pressed together, we would like to know by how much their centres approach. Each cylinder at a small contact is a half-plane, and its sinking at the contact is by this section determined up to a constant that depends on the size of the body. The approach (approach (pogrezanje)) \(\delta\) of cylinders therefore does not follow from the plane model. No choice repairs it: this is why for rollers the law \(Q \propto \delta^{10/9}\) of section 25.7 is fitted empirically, not derived (HK, PDF p. 156). For a three-dimensional contact the stiffness is well defined, for a two-dimensional one it is not (BOWER, PDF p. 330).

The line is not infinitely long. For a cylinder of length \(\ell\) the line of contact is not infinite, so the plane model holds only if the depth is small against \(\ell\). We can compute the quantity once we know the field of a point force, that is in section 25.4 (theorem 25.15). We state the result in advance. If we spread the force \(F'\ell = F\) over a line of length \(\ell\) and add the fields of the point forces, the stress under the centre at depth \(y\) equals the Flamant stress times \(\dfrac{1 + 6t^2}{(1 + 4t^2)^{3/2}}\), \(t = y/\ell\) (num-03.py, M2, the integral checked by differentiation and numerically). The expansion is \(1 - 6t^4\), so the difference is below \(1\,\%\) for \(t \leq 0{,}2\), and at \(t = 1\) the stress is only \(0{,}626\) of the Flamant one, at \(t = 2\) only \(0{,}357\) (figure 25.12).

Let us draw the strip of length \(\ell\) on the surface, over which the force \(F\) is spread. Under its centre we take the depth \(y\). The blue region reaches to \(0{,}2\,\ell\), and in it the plane solution holds to \(1\,\%\). On the right is the curve of the ratio: at \(y/\ell = 0{,}2\) it is \(0{,}993\) and at \(1{,}0\) it is \(0{,}626\). For a cylinder with \(\ell = 10\) mm the plane model is thus good to a depth of \(2\) mm. HK calls this edge loading (HK PDF p. 145-148): at the ends of the cylinder the pressure is larger than in the middle, which is why the cylinders are crowned, a matter we do not treat here (HK, PDF p. 147-148).

The plane solution is thus accurate only in the band of depths smaller than the length of the line. In it the stress and the displacement are fully determined by \(F'\), \(E^*\) and \(\nu^*\).

25.4 A point force on a half-space: the Boussinesq solution

In section 25.1 every point of the foundation acted on its own: under the beam, a displacement \(v\) produced a force \(k\,v\) per unit length, and neighbouring points did not know each other. A real foundation, the ground under a footing or the steel of the ring on which a ball rests, does not act like that. If we press on one point only, its surroundings sink as well, as a mattress sinks around a single fist. The question of this section is therefore: by how much does the surface of an elastic body sink at a distance \(r\) from the point where a force \(F\) presses, and what stresses does the force cause inside? We need the answer for the contact of two bodies, where we must know how an elastic body gives way under a pressure on a small part of its surface.

The body we take is a half-space (polprostor): all the points with \(z \geq 0\), with the plane \(z = 0\) as its surface. The name says that we cut space in two by a plane and kept one half. The half-space is a model of a body that is much larger than the region where we press: the distances at which we want the field are much smaller than the dimensions of the body, so the far edge of the body has no influence (for a force of \(1000\) N the normal stress at a depth of \(10\) mm below the force is only \(4{,}8\) MPa, as we shall compute below). The material is homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic, with modulus \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) (theorem 3.11), the strains are small and the surface is smooth and frictionless. Let us take the steel of the book, \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), and a force \(F = 1000\) N.

Let us draw figure 25.13, the left panel first. The surface is the horizontal line, the body is below it, and we measure the distance from the axis of the force with \(r\) along the surface. The force \(F\) presses downward at the point \(O\), so the arrow ends at \(O\), like any push. The axis \(z\) goes from \(O\) into the body, and \(R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\) is the distance of a point from \(O\). The letter \(R\) has another role later in the chapter, the radius of curvature, but in this section it is only a distance. We write the force \(F\), not \(P\), because we kept \(P\) for the load of the beam (section 25.1).

We shall first state and check the solution, not derive it, because the derivation with potentials (BARBER §23.2.1, PDF p. 372-374) goes beyond what the book has. Checking is an honest proof: we look for a displacement field that meets all the requirements, and verifying them is a calculation. We shall not prove uniqueness, see below the theorem.

Theorem 25.15 Boussinesq solution (Boussinesqova rešitev)

Let a half-space \(z \geq 0\) be made of a homogeneous, isotropic, linearly elastic material with \(E\) and \(\nu \neq -1\), \(\nu \neq \tfrac12\) (shear modulus \(G = E/(2(1 + \nu))\), definition 3.9), let \(F > 0\) and \(R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\). The displacement field

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{F}{4\pi G}\Big(\frac{x z}{R^3} - \frac{(1 - 2\nu)\,x}{R\,(R + z)}\Big) , \quad u_{\mathrm{y}} = \frac{F}{4\pi G}\Big(\frac{y z}{R^3} - \frac{(1 - 2\nu)\,y}{R\,(R + z)}\Big) , \quad u_{\mathrm{z}} = \frac{F}{4\pi G}\Big(\frac{2(1 - \nu)}{R} + \frac{z^2}{R^3}\Big) \tag{25.11}\]

has continuous second derivatives at every point with \(R > 0\) and \(z \geq 0\), and:

  1. it satisfies the Navier-Lamé equations (11.3) without body force,
  2. it has the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z^2}{2\pi R^5}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,y z^2}{2\pi R^5}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,z^3}{2\pi R^5}\), so on every plane \(z = c > 0\) the vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\) points along a line through \(O\) and has the length \(3F c^2/(2\pi R^4)\),
  3. the surface \(z = 0\) outside \(O\) is free of load, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\),
  4. on every plane \(z = c > 0\) the resultant of the stresses on the disc of radius \(\rho\) centred on the \(z\) axis has the components \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), and its component \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) tends to \(-F\) as \(\rho \to \infty\),
  5. the displacements of the surface are \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = \dfrac{F\,(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E\,r}\) and in the radial direction \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)(1 + \nu)\,F}{2\pi E\,r}\) (towards \(O\)), \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\),
  6. the displacements go to zero like \(1/R\) and the stresses like \(1/R^2\) as \(R \to \infty\).
Proof

We must show six claims. We compute the derivatives with the chain rule with \(\partial R/\partial x = x/R\), \(\partial R/\partial y = y/R\), \(\partial R/\partial z = z/R\) and simplify the expressions with \(R^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\), which is a calculation in SymPy (outlines/ch-kontakt-lezaji/num-04.py). One more relation is important, \((R + z)^2 = x^2 + y^2 + 2z^2 + 2Rz\).

  1. The fields (25.11) are made of powers of \(R\) and quotients with \(R + z\), which is positive on \(z \geq 0\) at \(R > 0\). So they have continuous second derivatives. The divergence is \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)\,F\,z}{2\pi G R^3}\) and its derivatives are \(\dfrac{\partial\operatorname{div}\vek u}{\partial x} = \dfrac{3(1 - 2\nu)F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5}\), the same for \(y\), and \(\dfrac{\partial\operatorname{div}\vek u}{\partial z} = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi G R^5}\).
  2. The Laplace operators (definition 11.5) of the components are \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5}\), the same for \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(y\), and \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{z}} = \dfrac{F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi G R^5}\).
  3. By theorem 11.6 we must show \(\mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{i}} + (\lambda + \mu)\,\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) with \(\mu = G\) and \(\lambda + \mu = G/(1 - 2\nu)\) (definition 3.10, \(\lambda = 2G\nu/(1 - 2\nu)\)). Component \(x\): \(G\cdot\Big(-\dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5}\Big) + \dfrac{G}{1 - 2\nu}\cdot\dfrac{3(1 - 2\nu)F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi R^5} + \dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi R^5} = 0\), the same for \(y\). Component \(z\): \(\dfrac{F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi R^5} - \dfrac{F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi R^5} = 0\). This is claim 1. We repeated the calculation exactly, with rational numbers, at the points \((1, 2, 2)\), \((2, 3, 6)\), \((4, 4, 7)\) and \((2, 6, 9)\), where \(R\) is the integer \(3\), \(7\), \(9\), \(11\), and got zero everywhere.
  4. We get the stresses from (11.4): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \lambda\operatorname{div}\vek u + 2G\,\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x)\). After differentiating and simplifying, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,z^3\,(R + z)^2}{2\pi R^5 (R + z)^2}\), because the numerator is \(2Rz + x^2 + y^2 + 2z^2 = (R + z)^2\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z^2}{2\pi R^5}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) the same. The vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}) = -\dfrac{3F z^2}{2\pi R^5}\,(x, y, z)\) is proportional to \((x, y, z)\), so it points along a line through \(O\), and on the plane \(z = c\) its length is \(\dfrac{3F c^2}{2\pi R^5}\,R = \dfrac{3F c^2}{2\pi R^4}\). This is claim 2.
  5. At \(z = 0\) all three stresses have the factor \(z^2\) and \(R = r > 0\), so they are zero. This is claim 3.
  6. For the plane \(z = c\) we use cylindrical coordinates (lemma 11.15, \(J = r\)) and theorem 4.59. On a disc of radius \(\rho\), \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -\dfrac{3F c^3}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\rho} \dfrac{r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta}{(r^2 + c^2)^{5/2}} = -3F c^3\Big[-\dfrac{1}{3(r^2 + c^2)^{3/2}}\Big]_0^{\rho} = -F\Big(1 - \dfrac{c^3}{(\rho^2 + c^2)^{3/2}}\Big)\), which tends to \(-F\) as \(\rho \to \infty\) (definition 9.16). For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) we have \(x = r\cos\theta\) and \(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 0\), the same for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) with \(\sin\theta\). This is claim 4.
  7. At \(z = 0\) we have \(R = r\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = \dfrac{F}{4\pi G}\cdot\dfrac{2(1 - \nu)}{r} = \dfrac{F(1 - \nu)}{2\pi G r}\). Since \(1/G = 2(1 + \nu)/E\), this is \(\dfrac{F(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E r}\). The radial component: \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -\dfrac{F(1 - 2\nu)\,x}{4\pi G\,r^2}\), the same for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(y\), so \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{F(1 - 2\nu)}{4\pi G\,r} = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)(1 + \nu)F}{2\pi E r}\). This is claim 5.
  8. Every term of (25.11) is divided by \(t\) when we replace \((x, y, z)\) by \((t x, t y, t z)\) with \(t > 0\), so \(\vek u(t\vek x) = \vek u(\vek x)/t\) (SymPy). Differentiating this equation with respect to \(x\) gives \(t\,\dfrac{\partial\vek u}{\partial x}(t\vek x) = \dfrac{1}{t}\,\dfrac{\partial\vek u}{\partial x}(\vek x)\), so the derivatives are divided by \(t^2\), likewise with respect to \(y\) and \(z\), and the stresses with them. For \(t = 1/R\) we get \(\vek u(\vek x) = \vek u(\vek x/R)/R\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek x) = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek x/R)/R^2\). The point \(\vek x/R\) lies on the hemisphere \(R = 1\), \(z \geq 0\), which is a closed and bounded set, and there \(R + z \geq 1\). So the displacements and stresses are continuous on it and by theorem 1.78 bounded by some constant \(M\). Hence \(|u_{\mathrm{i}}| \leq M/R\) and \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}| \leq M/R^2\). This is claim 6.

Source: BARBER §23.2.1, (23.14), (23.17), (23.18) (PDF p. 373-374): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) in the form \(3z^3/R^5\) with a potential of another normalisation, the surface displacements with proportionality \(1/r\) and the same factors \((1 - 2\nu)\) and \((1 - \nu)\). TIMO (PDF p. 268-269): the direction of the stress resultant towards the point of loading, the dependence \(1/R^2\) and \(w = P(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E r)\). We checked the field (25.11) in SymPy, the proof is a verification, it is not from the source. We do not prove uniqueness of the solution (see the text).

The proof showed that the field (25.11) solves the equations in the interior, that the surface is free of load everywhere except at the point \(O\), and that every plane below the surface carries the whole force \(F\). The last is what we expect of a point load: we cut off the part of the body above the plane \(z = c\) and the force \(F\) acts downward on it, so by the equilibrium of a part of a body (corollary 4.41, used here without proof on an unbounded part containing the point \(O\), so only as an expectation, the proof is step 6) the lower part must act with \(F\) upward, which with the normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) is exactly \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -F\).

We do not prove uniqueness. Theorem 11.4 holds for bounded bodies and smooth data, while the half-space is unbounded and a force at a point is not a smooth load (we do not prove uniqueness of the contact problem of an interference fit either, section 11.7.6, there because the contact pressure is not given). For the chosen solution it helps that the displacements and stresses decay (claim 6), and that the displacements depend on \(1/r\), which also follows from a dimensional argument (BARBER PDF p. 374), but this is not a proof of uniqueness.

From history

Joseph Valentin Boussinesq (1842-1929) was the most distinguished pupil of Saint-Venant (TIMO, PDF p. 267). In 1867 he took his doctorate and at about the same time wrote a treatise on the theory of elasticity, which Saint-Venant reviewed and at once recognised the young author as exceptional (TIMO, PDF p. 267). In 1873 he became a professor in Lille (TIMO, PDF p. 268). His most important works are collected in a book on the application of potentials to the equilibrium and motion of elastic bodies, published in Paris in 1885 (TIMO, PDF p. 268). Timoshenko writes that among his solutions the most important for practice are those of the stresses and deformations in a semi-infinite body due to known forces on the boundary plane (TIMO, PDF p. 268). In the simplest case the force acts perpendicular to the plane. Boussinesq found that the resultant of the stress on a horizontal plane points along the line through the loaded point and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from it (TIMO, PDF p. 268-269). For the vertical displacement of the boundary plane he obtained \(w = P(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E r)\), so the product \(w r\) is constant and the lines from the origin on the boundary turn into hyperbolas with the asymptotes \(Or\) and \(Oz\) after deformation (TIMO, PDF p. 269).

Let us return to the field (25.11): the historical result is claim 5 of the theorem, and the corollary is its special case.

Corollary 25.16 Deflection of the surface of a half-space (poves površja polprostora)

Under the conditions of theorem 25.15, for every \(r > 0\) the deflection of the surface is \(w(r) = u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, 0) = \dfrac{F\,(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E\,r}\), so the product \(w\,r = \dfrac{F\,(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E}\) is constant, the graph of \(w\) over \(r\) is a hyperbola with the asymptotes the \(r\)-axis and the \(z\)-axis, and \(w \to \infty\) as \(r \to 0\).

Proof

By claim 5 of theorem 25.15, \(u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, 0) = F(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E r)\). If \(w(r_1) = C/r_1\) and \(w(r_2) = C/r_2\), then \(w(r_1)\,r_1 = C = w(r_2)\,r_2\) for any two distances, so the rectangles \(r_1 \times w_1\) and \(r_2 \times w_2\) with the common vertex \(O\) and sides on the axes are not similar, but they have the same area \(C\). As \(r \to 0\) the denominator has the limit zero and the numerator is constant, so \(w\) grows beyond every bound.

Source: TIMO (PDF p. 269), BARBER (23.18) (PDF p. 374). The proof is a corollary of the theorem.

Let us look at this on the graph of the deflection in the left panel of figure 25.13: the blue curve is \(w = C/r\) and its value is read by the scale downward. Two rectangular areas are the same number \(C\): at \(r_1 = 1\) the deflection \(w_1\) is four times larger than the deflection \(w_2\) at \(r_2 = 4\), because \(r_2 = 4r_1\) and \(w r\) is constant. For our steel and the force \(1000\) N, \(C = F(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E) = 1{,}478 \cdot 10^{-9}\) m\(^2\), so \(w = 1{,}478\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(r = 1\) mm, \(0{,}148\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(10\) mm and \(14{,}78\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(0{,}1\) mm (SymPy, num-04.py). The radial displacement is towards \(O\) and is \(0{,}422\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(r = 1\) mm, so smaller than the deflection by the factor \((1 - 2\nu)/(2(1 - \nu)) = 0{,}286\).

It is also worth seeing how such a deflection arises. For the foundation of section 25.1 the displacement of a point of the foundation is the force per unit length with which the beam presses on the foundation at that point, divided by \(k\), so it depends only on that force. Here the deflection at the distance \(r\) depends on the force acting at the distance \(r\) away, and it decays only like \(1/r\), more slowly than for any foundation with only local stiffness. So for the half-space we shall have to add up the influence of the pressure from the whole region of contact.

Let us look at what the force does in the interior. The middle panel of figure 25.13 is a section of the body in true proportions. It shows the same surface and the same force \(F\) at the point \(O\) as on the left. The plane \(z = c\) is at the depth \(c\) below \(O\). We draw the dashed rays from \(O\) to chosen points of the plane, because by claim 2 of theorem 25.15 the stress resultant points along such lines. The orange arrows are the stresses that the part of the body above the plane transmits to the lower part. Each ends on the plane, on its own line, because they push the lower part downward, and their length falls with \((c/R)^4\), so quickly as we move away from the axis: at \(r = c\) the length is \(0{,}25\) of the length on the axis, and at \(r = 2c\) it is \(0{,}04\) (by \(3F c^2/(2\pi R^4)\), SymPy). The right panel shows only the vertical component: horizontally \(r/c\), vertically \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}|\) divided by its value on the axis. The bell is \((1 + (r/c)^2)^{-5/2}\), the stress \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}| = \dfrac{3F}{2\pi c^2}\big(1 + (r/c)^2\big)^{-5/2}\) divided by its value on the axis. When we rotate the area under the bell for the undivided stress about the axis, the solid obtained has by claim 4 the volume \(F\). At \(c = 5\) mm and \(F = 1000\) N, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) on the axis is \(-19{,}10\) MPa, at \(r = 5\) mm \(-3{,}376\) MPa, at \(10\) mm \(-0{,}342\) MPa and at \(15\) mm \(-0{,}060\) MPa. So at the depth \(c\) the load spreads over a disc of radius a few times \(c\). We trust the field of a point force as a stand-in for a pressure on a small region only at a distance much larger than the size of the region (at a distance of two radii of a loaded disc the difference is \(3{,}5\ \%\), at six radii \(0{,}35\ \%\), as we shall see below).

How close to \(O\) we may trust linear theory itself is told by the size of the derivatives of the displacements. On the surface the largest are \(|\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial r| = |\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial z| = C/r^2\), the others are smaller or zero (SymPy). At \(r = 1\) mm this is \(1{,}5\cdot 10^{-3}\), at \(r = 0{,}3\) mm it is \(1{,}6\cdot 10^{-2}\) and at \(r = 0{,}1\) mm it is \(0{,}148\). Linear theory assumes that all derivatives of the displacements are below about \(0{,}001\) in size (section 3.2.1, assumption 4), so for our force it holds for \(r \gtrsim 1{,}2\) mm, \(r = \sqrt{C/0{,}001}\).

Near the point of loading. As \(r \to 0\) the deflection goes beyond every bound (corollary 25.16), and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) on the axis goes as \(1/z^2\) as \(z \to 0\). This is not a mistake of the solution but a measure of the model: a force at one point means infinite pressure, because pressure is force over area and the area is zero. No steel bears such a pressure, so the model stops being used long before infinity is put into the calculation, at the yield limit. Timoshenko writes that we can help ourselves by cutting out the material near the point with a hemispherical surface of small radius and replacing the force by statically equivalent forces distributed over this surface (TIMO, PDF p. 269). The second way out, which we shall use, means the same: the force acts on a finite region of the surface, as a pressure.

25.4.1 Pressure on a finite region

Let the force act not at a point but as a pressure \(p\) on a region \(A\) of the surface. Pressure (tlak) is a function of a point of the surface: at the point \(s \in A\) the number \(p(s)\) is the force per unit area in N/m\(^2\) (in MPa), and the force on a part \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\) of the region is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\) over a set with an area (definition 4.30). The sum over the parts is the whole force \(F = \int_{\mathrm{A}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\). We know how the surface sinks only for a point force, so we cut the region into finitely many parts, replace the force of each part by a point force and add the fields by the principle of superposition. Does the sum settle as the parts become ever smaller? Figure 25.14 (left) shows what we draw for the proof.

First the disc of radius \(a\) and centre \(O\): the region on which the pressure acts. In it is the point \(x\), at which we look for the deflection. If \(x\) lies outside the region, the function \(1/|x - s|\) is continuous on it, which we shall use in step 2. If it lies inside, the function is unbounded as \(s \to x\). So from \(x\) we draw a sector between two rays, where the distance \(\rho = |x - s|\) varies from zero to the edge, and write the integral in polar coordinates around \(x\), where the factor \(\rho\) from the Jacobian determinant just cancels \(1/\rho\). The length of this ray up to the edge is the chord \(\ell(\varphi)\) at the angle \(\varphi\).

Lemma 25.17 Deflection under a pressure (poves pod tlakom)

The material and model as in theorem 25.15. Let \(A\) be a closed convex set with an area on the surface \(z = 0\) (a disc, an ellipse, a rectangle) of diameter \(D\) (the diameter of a set is the largest distance between two of its points), and \(p \geq 0\) a continuous pressure function on \(A\), \(p \leq p_{\max}\), \(F = \int_{\mathrm{A}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\). For a point \(x\) of the surface we denote

\[w(x) = \frac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\int_{\mathrm{A}} \frac{p(s)}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}A(s) . \tag{25.12}\]
  1. If \(x\) has the distance \(d > 0\) from \(A\) and we cut \(A\) into parts \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{n}}\) of diameter at most \(h\), with points \(s_{\mathrm{j}} \in A_{\mathrm{j}}\) and forces \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\), the deflection of the surface at \(x\) due to the point forces \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) at \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x) = \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dfrac{F_{\mathrm{j}}}{|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|}\) and \(\big|w_{\mathrm{n}}(x) - w(x)\big| \leq \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\cdot\dfrac{F\,h}{d^2}\).
  2. If \(x\) lies in \(A\), the integrand is unbounded at \(s = x\), so there the integral (25.12) means the limit of the integrals over \(A\) without the disc of radius \(\varepsilon\) around \(x\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). This limit exists and in polar coordinates around \(x\) it is \(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\ell(\varphi)} p\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\), where \(\ell(\varphi) \leq D\) is the length of the ray to the edge, and hence \(w(x) \leq \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\,2\pi D\,p_{\max}\).
Proof

We must show an estimate for a point outside and finiteness for a point inside the region.

  1. The field of the point force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) at \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the field (25.11), shifted to \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\). By theorem 25.15 it satisfies the equations, and by corollary 11.3 (its proof uses only the linearity of derivatives and of Hooke's law, so it holds for the half-space as well) the sum of the fields is a field with displacements and stresses that are the same sums. On the surface, by corollary 25.16, the displacement is \(F_{\mathrm{j}}(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E\,|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|)\), which gives \(w_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  2. For every \(j\) the difference \(\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A - F_{\mathrm{j}}/|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|\) equals \(\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p(s)\big(\dfrac{1}{|x - s|} - \dfrac{1}{|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|}\big)\mathrm{d}A\), because \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\). Since \(|x - s|\) and \(|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|\) are both at least \(d\) and differ by at most \(|s - s_{\mathrm{j}}| \leq h\), \(\Big|\dfrac{1}{|x - s|} - \dfrac{1}{|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|}\Big| = \dfrac{\big||x - s_{\mathrm{j}}| - |x - s|\big|}{|x - s|\,|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|} \leq \dfrac{h}{d^2}\). So the difference is \(|\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A - F_{\mathrm{j}}/|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|| \leq F_{\mathrm{j}}\,h/d^2\). We add over \(j\) and use \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} F_{\mathrm{j}} = F\) (additivity of the integral over a set). This is the estimate of claim 1. As \(h \to 0\) the right side tends to zero, so \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x)\) tends to \(w(x)\).
  3. For \(x \in A\) we take \(A\) without the disc of radius \(\varepsilon\) around \(x\). Since \(A\) is convex, the set of points of \(A\) on the ray at the angle \(\varphi\) from \(x\) is a segment \(0 \leq \rho \leq \ell(\varphi)\) with \(\ell \leq D\). In polar coordinates around \(x\), \(J = \rho\) (theorem 4.59, \(\Phi(\rho, \varphi) = x + \rho\,(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)\)), so \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_\varepsilon^{\ell(\varphi)} (p/\rho)\,\rho\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\), where \(\rho\) cancels \(1/\rho\) (where \(\ell(\varphi) < \varepsilon\), the inner integral is zero).
  4. The integrand \(p\) is continuous and bounded by \(p_{\max}\), and \(\ell(\varphi) \leq D\), so the integral \(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\ell(\varphi)} p\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\) exists and is at most \(2\pi D\,p_{\max}\). It differs from the integral of step 3 by the integral over \(0 \leq \rho \leq \varepsilon\), which is at most \(2\pi\varepsilon\,p_{\max}\) and tends to zero as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). So the limit exists and equals this integral. This is claim 2.

Source: TIMO (PDF p. 269): Boussinesq solves a load distributed over a part of the boundary plane by the principle of superposition. The proof is not from the source. For a point inside the region we do not prove that the value of the integral is the value of the true solution for a pressure, but take it as a definition and check it against TIMO on the example of a disc below (cited, not proved).

The proof showed two things: for points outside the region the sum of point forces does settle at the integral, with an error estimate proportional to \(h\), and for points inside the integral is finite although the integrand has a singularity. This is exactly what the point force lacks.

Uniform pressure on a disc. Let \(p = q\) be constant on a disc of radius \(a\). For \(x\) at the centre, \(\ell(\varphi) = a\) for every \(\varphi\) and by claim 2, \(\int_0^{2\pi} a\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = 2\pi a\), so \(w(0) = \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\,q\,2\pi a = \dfrac{2(1 - \nu^2)\,q\,a}{E}\). For \(x\) on the edge, with \(\varphi\) measured from the direction towards the centre, \(\ell(\varphi) = 2a\cos\varphi\) for \(|\varphi| < \pi/2\) and zero elsewhere, so \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 2a\cos\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = 4a\) and \(w(a) = \dfrac{4(1 - \nu^2)\,q\,a}{\pi E} = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\,w(0)\). TIMO (PDF p. 269) gives the same two numbers: \(w_0 = 2(1 - \nu^2)\,q\,a/E\) at the centre and \(2w_0/\pi\) at the edge. Our calculation gives them without quoting, so this is a verification of that claim (SymPy and NumPy, num-04.py). Let us take \(F = 1000\) N on a disc of radius \(a = 1\) mm, \(q = F/(\pi a^2) = 318{,}3\) MPa: \(w(0) = 2{,}956\ \mu\text{m}\), \(w(a) = 1{,}882\ \mu\text{m}\), and the point force would give \(1{,}478\ \mu\text{m}\) at the distance \(a\). The right panel of figure 25.14 shows the course of the deflection divided by the deflection at the centre, over \(r/a\): the blue curve is the deflection of the disc, at the edge it is \(2/\pi = 0{,}637\) of the deflection at the centre, and the orange curve is the deflection of the point force at the centre. At \(r = 2a\) the disc is \(3{,}5\ \%\) above the point force (\(0{,}7645\) against \(0{,}7389\ \mu\text{m}\)), and at \(r = 6a\) only \(0{,}35\ \%\), as we expect: from far away we cannot see whether the force acts at a point or on a small disc.

Sum and integral. Let us check the estimate of claim 1 at \(x\) at the distance \(2a\) from the centre, where \(d = a\), with \(a = 1\) mm and \(F = 1000\) N. We divide the plane into small squares of side \(2a/n\). The part \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the intersection of a square with the disc, its force is \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = q\) times the area of the part, the point \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the centroid of the part, and the forces add up to \(F\). The exact value is \(w(2a) = 0{,}7645\ \mu\text{m}\) and the deviation of the sum \(w_{\mathrm{n}}\) at \(n = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\) is \(-1{,}49\ \%\), \(-0{,}33\ \%\), \(-0{,}081\ \%\), \(-0{,}021\ \%\), \(-0{,}0049\ \%\), \(-0{,}0013\ \%\) (NumPy, areas and centroids approximately from \(200 \times 200\) points in each square). The estimate of claim 1 gives at most \(8{,}5\ \%\) at \(n = 64\) (the diameter of a part is at most \(h = \sqrt{2}\cdot 2a/64\)), while the actual deviation \(0{,}0013\ \%\) is much smaller: it falls by about a factor of four at each halving of the side, the estimate only by a factor of two. The estimate is therefore reliable but coarse. It falls with \(h\), which is what we need.

The point force is not a limit. Let us take the same force \(F = 1000\) N on an ever smaller disc: \(a = 1\) mm gives \(w(0) = 2{,}956\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(q = 318\) MPa, \(a = 0{,}1\) mm gives \(29{,}56\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(q = 31\,830\) MPa, \(a = 0{,}01\) mm gives \(295{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(q = 3{,}18\cdot 10^6\) MPa. The product \(w(0)\,a = 2(1 - \nu^2)F/(\pi E) = 2C\) is constant, so \(w(0) = 2C/a \to \infty\) as \(a \to 0\), as for a point force. So the deflection has no finite limit as \(a \to 0\), and we must not regard the point force as the limiting case of contact. Contact requires a finite region, which we do not know in advance, since it depends on the deflection. This will be the task of the following sections.

25.5 Hertz contact of two cylinders: the contact conditions and line contact

At the end of section 25.4 we found that a point force cannot be a model of contact: the deflection under it is infinite, and the pressure is infinite for every finite force. A contact needs a region of finite size, which we do not know in advance, because the deflection itself determines it. In a roller bearing such a contact is met at every step: a roller, a steel cylinder with a radius of a few millimetres, lies on a raceway, and the raceway pushes it with a force that the bearing has to carry. The question of this section is therefore: how wide is the strip along which roller and raceway touch, how large is the pressure in it, and how does the load connect them? We start with two cylinders, because this is a plane problem, and for the plane we have Flamant's solution (theorem 25.13). The ball, which needs a three-dimensional solution after Boussinesq, is treated in section 25.6.

Let us draw figure 25.15, first the left half. We take the lower body, whose surface bulges upwards with radius \(R_2\). It stands for a piece of the raceway under the roller, and we need its flat lower face only to have something to rest it on. On it we place the upper cylinder with radius \(R_1\), whose axis is perpendicular to the plane of the drawing. It is drawn as a circle because we look at a cross-section, and both bodies have the same length along the axis, which is much larger than everything in the cross-section. Therefore nothing changes along the axis and the plane of the drawing tells everything (plane strain, definition 11.30). The bodies are pressed together by the forces \(F'\): the upper cylinder pushes down, the lower body pushes up, both along the line through the centres. The prime on \(F'\) is not a derivative, it says that this is the force per unit length of the axis (sila na enoto dolžine), in N/m, in numbers in N/mm. The bodies touch at the point of the cross-section on this line, which in space is a line along the whole length of the axis. For this reason we call it a line contact (črtni stik).

Before we compute, let us say when the model is good. For a steel roller we take \(R_1 = 5\) mm on a raceway with radius \(R_2 = 25\) mm and \(F' = 100\) N/mm. Below we will compute that the contact strip is \(0{,}14\) mm wide, which is \(2{,}8\ \%\) of the radius of the roller. This is what we need: the strip is small compared with the bodies, so in computing the stresses near the contact we can take each body to be a half-plane, as if the surface were infinite.

Definition 25.18 Nonconformal contact (nekonformni stik)

A contact of two bodies is nonconformal if it has three properties:

  1. Before loading the bodies touch at a point or along a line.
  2. Both bodies are smooth near the contact, so that their local shape can be described by convex surfaces (here a cylinder or a sphere).
  3. The contact patch is much smaller than both bodies.

The name says the opposite: in a conformal contact (konformni stik) the bodies fit each other, like a ball in a groove of almost the same radius, and the contact patch is already large at a small load. Such a contact is treated in section 25.6. In addition we take the bodies to be linearly elastic, isotropic and homogeneous, the strains to be small, and the contact to be frictionless, so that only normal forces act on the contact surface (BOWER, section 5.4.11, PDF p. 333).

Source: BOWER §5.4.11 (PDF p. 333): "(1) the two contacting solids initially touch at a point or along a line, (2) both contacting solids are smooth in the neighborhood of the contact, so that their local geometry can be approximated as ellipsoids, and (3) the size of the contact patch between the two solids is much smaller than either solid." Frictionless contact is assumed there too (same place). For surface shear see HK §6.5 (PDF pp. 139-142), which we do not treat here.

Property 3 is an inequality that we must check, and we will: for our numbers \(b/R_1 = 0{,}014\), and at four times the load \(0{,}028\). Property 1 tells where we start: as the load grows, the point or line of contact widens into a strip. The point force of section 25.4 is the limiting case of a strip squeezed into a point, and since it would give an infinite pressure, we must replace it by a strip of finite width.

The contact strip (stična ožina) is the set of points where the surfaces touch, and we do not know which points these are. So we describe it with two functions. Let \(x\) be the coordinate along the common tangent at the point of touching, measured in the plane of the cross-section. The gap (zazor) \(g(x)\) is the distance between the surfaces at the coordinate \(x\), measured in the direction of the force. The pressure (tlak) \(p(x)\) is the normal force per area of the contact surface that the bodies exert on each other, in N/m\(^2\), in numbers in MPa. By Newton's third law body 1 acts on body 2 with the same force as body 2 on body 1, so on both surfaces we have the same \(p\). The force per unit length of the axis is then \(\int p\,\mathrm{d}x\) over the contact strip.

Definition 25.19 Contact conditions (stična pogoja)

Let two bodies that are in contact before loading be loaded by a force \(F' > 0\) per unit length. The unknowns are the functions of gap \(g\) and pressure \(p\) on the line of contact, both with values in \(\mathbb{R}\). The contact problem (stični problem) requires that for every \(x\):

  1. \(g(x) \geq 0\): the bodies do not penetrate each other.
  2. \(p(x) \geq 0\): the contact does not pull, the surfaces only push each other.
  3. \(g(x)\,p(x) = 0\): there is pressure only where the gap is zero, and the gap is larger than zero only where there is no pressure.
  4. \(\int p(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = F'\): the pressure carries the whole force.

The set \(\Omega = \{x : g(x) = 0\}\) is the contact set (stična množica). Besides \(p\) and \(g\) we must determine it, and for this very reason the contact problem is not linear: for a given \(F'\) we cannot add the solutions for two different sets \(\Omega\).

Source: BARBER §12.5.3 (PDF p. 195), inequalities (12.48) "contact traction should not be tensile" and (12.49) "no interference between the bodies outside the contact area". The complete form with requirement (3) is my formulation of both. Uniqueness of the solution is not proved (see the remark below theorem 25.24).

Let us compare this with the previous example of a contact. In the shrink fit of tubes (section 11.7.6) the contact was on the whole cylindrical surface, so \(\Omega\) was known and only the pressure \(p_{\mathrm{c}}\) was unknown. Uniqueness of the contact problem itself, where \(p_{\mathrm{c}}\) is not given, was not proved there, and it is not proved here either. For the cylinders in the figure we do not know in advance how wide the strip is: the deformation itself decides it.

The gap after loading consists of three parts: the gap of the undeformed bodies \(g_0\), the movement of the bodies towards each other, and the elastic displacements of the surfaces. First the first part.

Lemma 25.20 Gap of two cylinders (zazor dveh valjev)

Let two cylinders with radii \(R_1, R_2 > 0\) be convex, touching at the point \(O\) of the cross-section where \(x = 0\). The gap of the undeformed cylinders at the distance \(x\) from \(O\), \(|x| \leq \min(R_1, R_2)\), is

\[g_0(x) = \big(R_1 - \sqrt{R_1^2 - x^2}\big) + \big(R_2 - \sqrt{R_2^2 - x^2}\big) , \tag{25.13}\]

and it satisfies

\[\frac{x^2}{2R} \leq g_0(x) \leq \frac{x^2}{2R}\Big(1 + \frac{x^2}{R_{\min}^2}\Big) , \qquad \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} , \tag{25.14}\]

where \(R_{\min} = \min(R_1, R_2)\).

Proof

We must show that \(g_0\) is the sum of the offsets of two circles from the common tangent, and estimate each.

  1. A circle with radius \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) that touches the tangent at \(O\) has its centre on the normal at \(O\) at the distance \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\). Its point at the distance \(x\) from the normal is at the distance \(R_{\mathrm{i}} - \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2}\) from the tangent by Pythagoras' theorem. The bodies lie on the two sides of the tangent, so the gap is the sum of the two offsets, which is (25.13).
  2. For each offset we extend the fraction: \(R_{\mathrm{i}} - \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2} = x^2/(R_{\mathrm{i}} + \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2})\).
  3. Lower bound. Since \(\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2} \leq R_{\mathrm{i}}\), the denominator is at most \(2R_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the offset is at least \(x^2/(2R_{\mathrm{i}})\).
  4. Upper bound. For \(q = |x|/R_{\mathrm{i}} \leq 1\) we have \(\sqrt{1 - q^2} \geq 1 - q^2\), because \(1 - q^2 \geq (1 - q^2)^2 = 1 - 2q^2 + q^4\) exactly when \(q^2 \geq q^4\). So the denominator is at least \(R_{\mathrm{i}}(2 - q^2)\) and the offset at most \(\dfrac{x^2}{R_{\mathrm{i}}(2 - q^2)} = \dfrac{x^2}{2R_{\mathrm{i}}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1 - q^2/2} \leq \dfrac{x^2}{2R_{\mathrm{i}}}(1 + q^2)\), because \(1/(1 - u) \leq 1 + 2u\) for \(0 \leq u \leq \tfrac12\) (here \(u = q^2/2 \leq \tfrac12\)).
  5. We add the two offsets: the lower bound is \(\tfrac{x^2}{2}(1/R_1 + 1/R_2) = x^2/(2R)\), the upper bound is \(\tfrac{x^2}{2R}(1 + q_{\max}^2)\) with \(q_{\max} = |x|/R_{\min}\), because \(q_{\mathrm{i}} \leq q_{\max}\).

Source: The computation is mine. BARBER §12.6 (PDF p. 197) takes the radii to be large compared with the contact width, \(R_1, R_2 \gg a\), and describes the gap by a known function \(h(x)\). Our estimate tells how large the correction is.

For our roller and raceway at \(x = b = 70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\) the largest relative error is \(\big(b/R_1\big)^2 = 2{,}0\cdot 10^{-4}\), and the actual error of a single circular offset, for example for \(R_1\), at \(x = b\) is only \(4{,}9\cdot 10^{-5}\) (SymPy, num-05.py). In the contact strip we may therefore write the gap of the undeformed bodies as \(g_0 = x^2/(2R)\), a parabola, and this is the gap of one cylinder with radius \(R\) against a plane. For what follows we need one more number: both bodies deform under load, and their elasticity must enter in a single number.

Definition 25.21 Effective modulus and effective radius of contact (efektivni modul in polmer stika)

For two bodies in contact with moduli \(E_1, E_2\), Poisson ratios \(\nu_1, \nu_2\) and radii \(R_1, R_2\) we define the numbers \(E^*\) and \(R\) by

\[\frac{1}{E^*} = \frac{1 - \nu_1^2}{E_1} + \frac{1 - \nu_2^2}{E_2} , \qquad \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} . \tag{25.15}\]

Both are numbers with the units Pa and m. If the surface of a body is convex, its radius is positive, if it is concave, negative (BOWER, PDF p. 333, and the treatment in section 25.6).

Source: BOWER §5.4.11 (PDF pp. 333-334): "effective modulus" and "effective contact radius". HK (6.51) (PDF p. 132): \(b = \big[\tfrac{4Q}{\pi l\,\Sigma\rho}\big(\tfrac{1 - \xi_{\mathrm{I}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{I}}} + \tfrac{1 - \xi_{\mathrm{II}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{II}}}\big)\big]^{1/2}\) contains the same sum \((1 - \xi^2)/E\) and \(\Sigma\rho = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2\).

Three warnings about notation. The letter \(E^*\) is here an italic number, while in the chapter on deformation the bold \(\mat E^*\) is the Euler-Almansi tensor, a different object. In section 25.3, \(E^* = E/(1 - \nu^2)\) was the modulus of one body in plane strain (corollary 11.34). The effective modulus extends it to two bodies: if the second body is rigid (\(E_2 \to \infty\)), then \(E^* = E_1/(1 - \nu_1^2)\), the same number. For two equal bodies, however, it is half as large, because (25.15) has two equal terms \((1 - \nu^2)/E\) instead of one. The letter \(R\) is the radius of the contact, not to be confused with the distance \(R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\) of section 25.4. For two steel bodies of the book (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\)) we have \(E^* = E/(2(1 - \nu^2)) = 107{,}692\) GPa, because both sums are equal and each is \((1 - \nu^2)/E\). For the roller and the raceway \(R = 4{,}1667\) mm.

Now we can look at the right half of figure 25.15. The equivalent problem is drawn: a half-plane with modulus \(E^*\) replaces both elastic bodies, and a rigid cylinder with radius \(R\) and the same force \(F'\) replaces the gap \(g_0 = x^2/(2R)\). The horizontal and the vertical coordinate are drawn with the axes, as in sections 25.3 and 25.4. Whether the problem is really equivalent is shown by the computation of displacements below: the displacements of the surfaces of the two bodies add up in the gap, and their sum has the same form as for a half-plane with modulus \(E^*\).

Why such a sum appears we see when we compute the deflection that a pressure causes on the half-plane. Flamant's solution (lemma 25.14) gives, for a force \(F\) per unit length at the point \(s\), the deflection of the surface of the half-plane into the body \(-\dfrac{2(1 - \nu^2)\,F}{\pi E}\ln|x - s| + \text{const.}\), where the constant does not depend on \(x\). We cut the pressure \(p\) on the interval \([-b, b]\) into pieces \([s_{\mathrm{j}}, s_{\mathrm{j}} + h]\) with forces \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = \int p\,\mathrm{d}s\) over the piece and add the contributions by the principle of superposition (corollary 11.3). The limit of the Riemann sums is an integral (as in lemma 25.17, where here the kernel \(\ln|x - s|\) is integrable even at \(s \to x\)). We state it in a lemma.

Lemma 25.22 Surface deflection under a line pressure (poves površja pod črtnim tlakom)

Let the bodies of definition 25.18 be in plane strain with constant \(E_{\mathrm{i}}, \nu_{\mathrm{i}}\), and let \(p \geq 0\) be a continuous function on \((-b, b)\) that is zero outside and has the integral (improper if needed, definition 9.16) \(\int p\,\mathrm{d}s = F'\). The sum of the displacements \(w = w_1 + w_2\) of the surfaces of the bodies into each body, caused by \(p\), is

\[w(x) = -\frac{2}{\pi E^*}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b} p(s)\,\ln|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}s + C_0 , \tag{25.16}\]

where \(C_0\) does not depend on \(x\) (and is undetermined, see lemma 25.25), and

  1. for \(|x| > b\) we have \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\displaystyle\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{p(s)}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s\), an ordinary integral,
  2. for \(|x| < b\) we have \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\,\mathrm{PV}\displaystyle\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{p(s)}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s\), the principal value (glavna vrednost) \(\mathrm{PV}\displaystyle\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b} f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\Big(\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{x - \varepsilon} + \int_{\mathrm{x} + \varepsilon}^{b}\Big) f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
Proof

We must show the form (25.16) and both expressions for the derivative.

  1. Each body is a half-plane. By lemma 25.14 the deflection of the surface under a force \(F\) at the point \(s\) is \(-\tfrac{2(1 - \nu_{\mathrm{i}}^2)F}{\pi E_{\mathrm{i}}}\ln|x - s| + \text{const.}\) (checked in SymPy, num-05.py, part A: it satisfies Hooke's law and the relation between strains and displacements, residual zero). Both bodies carry the same force \(F\) at the point \(s\) by Newton's third law.
  2. The sum of the deflections of the two bodies has the factor \(2\big((1 - \nu_1^2)/E_1 + (1 - \nu_2^2)/E_2\big)/\pi = 2/(\pi E^*)\) by definition 25.21. Superposition and the passage to the limit of the Riemann sums (lemma 25.17 for point forces, the argument is the same) give (25.16).
  3. For \(|x| > b\) the function \(x \mapsto \ln|x - s|\) is smooth for \(s \in [-b, b]\) with the derivative \(1/(x - s)\) in \(s\) and \(x\), so we may differentiate under the integral (lemma 4.19). This is claim 1.
  4. For \(|x| < b\) the integrand in claim 2 has a pole at \(s = x\), so the expression is an ordinary integral only as a principal value. That this is really the derivative is a result of BARBER (12.27), (12.28) (PDF p. 190), which we quote without proof. For the case we need, we check it in step 3 of the proof of theorem 25.24 by computing the displacement itself (NumPy, num-05.py, part G).

Source: BARBER §12.3.1 (PDF p. 188, (12.12) to (12.20)) and §12.4 (PDF pp. 189-190, (12.26) to (12.28)): the deflection under a distributed pressure as an integral of the Flamant kernel, logarithmically unbounded far from the contact, and therefore the formulation of contact problems with the derivative (12.27), in which, for a point inside the region, the integral is a Cauchy principal value. Claim 2 is therefore quoted and not proved.

The proof showed two things: the displacement depends on the logarithm of the distance, so it is determined only up to a constant (this will matter at the end of the section), while its derivative is determined and we need it. The derivative is an integral with a pole, which we must compute for the half-ellipse, and so let us first say what the pole does.

Let us draw figure 25.16. On the axis \(s\) there is the interval \([-b, b]\), bounded by the vertical lines at \(\pm b\), where the pressure vanishes. The point where we compute the slope we mark with \(x\), in the figure \(x = 0{,}4\,b\). There the integrand has a pole, because the denominator \(x - s\) becomes zero. The left branch lies to the left of the pole, where \(x - s > 0\), so the value grows beyond every bound as \(s\) approaches \(x\). The right branch lies to the right, where \(x - s < 0\), and goes to \(-\infty\). Each branch alone has an infinite area, but the sum need not be infinite. So we cut out the interval \((x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon)\) with the half-width \(\varepsilon\) on both sides and take the limit \(\varepsilon \to 0\). With such a symmetric cut-out the infinities cancel each other. With an asymmetric cut-out, for example \((x - \varepsilon, x + 2\varepsilon)\), the value would change by \(\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}\,\ln 2\), which at \(x = 0{,}4\,b\) equals \(0{,}635\,b\), and this is large compared with the true value \(\pi x = 1{,}257\,b\). Without an agreement on the cut-out the integral therefore has no value, and this agreement is the principal value.

Lemma 25.23 Integrals of the half-circle with a pole (integrali polkroga s polom)

Let \(b > 0\). If \(|x| < b\), then

\[\mathrm{PV}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0 , \qquad \mathrm{PV}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s = \pi x . \tag{25.17}\]

If \(x > b\), both integrals are ordinary and

\[\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}} , \qquad \int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s = \pi\big(x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}\big) . \tag{25.18}\]
Proof

We must show four values. The key is that \(1/((x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2})\) has elementary antiderivatives, different for \(x\) inside and outside the interval.

  1. Let \(|x| < b\) and \(c = \sqrt{b^2 - x^2} > 0\). We denote \(N(s) = b^2 - x s + c\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\) and \(H(s) = \dfrac{1}{c}\ln\dfrac{N(s)}{|x - s|}\). The derivative is \(H'(s) = \dfrac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\) on every interval where \(s \neq x\) (checked in SymPy, num-05.py, part B, residual \(10^{-16}\) at three points).
  2. At the end points \(N(b) = b(b - x)\) and \(|x - b| = b - x\), so \(N(b)/|x - b| = b\). Similarly \(N(-b) = b(b + x)\) and \(|x + b| = b + x\), so \(N(-b)/|x + b| = b\). Hence \(H(b) = H(-b) = \tfrac1c\ln b\) (num-05.py, part B, values \(1{,}0\)).
  3. The integral over the region with the cut-out is \(\big[H(x - \varepsilon) - H(-b)\big] + \big[H(b) - H(x + \varepsilon)\big]\) by steps 1 and 2 \(= H(x - \varepsilon) - H(x + \varepsilon) = \dfrac{1}{c}\ln\dfrac{N(x - \varepsilon)}{N(x + \varepsilon)}\), since \(|x - s| = \varepsilon\) cancels on both sides. The function \(N\) is continuous at \(s = x\) with the value \(N(x) = 2c^2 > 0\), so the ratio tends to \(1\) and the value to \(0\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). For \(b = 1\), \(x = 0{,}4\) the value is \(0{,}1047\), \(0{,}01039\), \(0{,}001039\), \(0{,}0001039\) at \(\varepsilon = 10^{-1}, \dots, 10^{-4}\), so proportional to \(\varepsilon\). This is the first value in (25.17).
  4. For the second value we write \(b^2 - s^2 = (b^2 - x^2) + (x - s)(x + s)\). Therefore \(\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s} = \dfrac{c^2}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}} + \dfrac{x + s}{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\).
  5. The principal value of the first term is \(0\) by step 3. The second term, with the substitution \(s = b\sin\varphi\) by theorem 4.59 (the Jacobian factor \(b\cos\varphi\), and \(\sqrt{b^2 - s^2} = b\cos\varphi\), which cancels), equals \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(x + b\sin\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = \pi x\), because \(\sin\) is odd. The second term has no pole at \(s = x\), so no cut-out is needed and the integral is ordinary (improper at \(\pm b\), definition 9.16). This is the second value in (25.17).
  6. Let \(x > b\) and \(c' = \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}\). We denote \(K(s) = \dfrac{1}{c'}\arctan\dfrac{b^2 - x s}{c'\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\). The derivative is \(K'(s) = -\dfrac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\) on \((-b, b)\) (num-05.py, part B). As \(s \to b\) the argument has the value \(b(b - x)/0 \to -\infty\) and as \(s \to -b\) the value \(b(b + x)/0 \to +\infty\), so \(K(b) = -\pi/(2c')\) and \(K(-b) = \pi/(2c')\). The integral is \(K(-b) - K(b) = \pi/c'\) (improper integral, definition 9.16). This is the first value in (25.18).
  7. With the split of step 4 the second integral is \(c^2\cdot\pi/c' + \pi x\) with \(c^2 = b^2 - x^2 = -c'^2\), so \(-\pi c' + \pi x\). This is the second value in (25.18).

Source: The computation is mine, the pattern with an antiderivative with a pole is a standard technique (BARBER, §12.5, PDF pp. 191-196, solves the same integral with Fourier series). We check the antiderivatives in SymPy, the numerical principal value agrees to \(10^{-8}\) (num-05.py, part C): \(\pi x\) at \(x/b = 0{,}3, 0{,}6, 0{,}9\) and \(\pi(x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2})\) at \(x/b = 1{,}2, 2, 5\).

The proof showed that the pressure \(p_0\sqrt{1 - s^2/b^2}\) gives a straight line in \(x\) in the expression for the slope. The gap is zero in the contact if its derivative is zero, and the theorem meets this with the choice of \(p_0\).

Theorem 25.24 Hertz line contact of cylinders (Hertzov črtni stik valjev)

Let the bodies of definition 25.18 be two convex cylinders with radii \(R_1, R_2\) in plane strain with effective modulus \(E^*\) and radius \(R\) (definition 25.21), pressed together by a force \(F' > 0\) per unit length. Let the gap of the undeformed bodies be \(g_0(x) = x^2/(2R)\) (lemma 25.20) and the gap after loading

\[g(x) = \frac{x^2}{2R} + w(x) - \delta , \tag{25.19}\]

where \(w\) is from lemma 25.22 and \(\delta\) is a number still unknown (the approach, explained below lemma 25.25). Let

\[b = \sqrt{\frac{4F'R}{\pi E^*}} , \qquad p_0 = \frac{2F'}{\pi b} = \frac{E^*\,b}{2R} = \sqrt{\frac{F'E^*}{\pi R}} , \qquad p(x) = \begin{cases} p_0\sqrt{1 - x^2/b^2} & |x| \leq b \\ 0 & |x| > b . \end{cases} \tag{25.20}\]

Then:

  1. The functions \(p\) and \(g\) satisfy the contact conditions of definition 25.19 with \(\Omega = [-b, b]\) for a suitable value of \(\delta\).
  2. Outside the contact \(g(x) = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\,G(|x|/b)\) with \(G(t) = \tfrac12\big(t\sqrt{t^2 - 1} - \ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\big)\), which is positive for \(t > 1\), and \(g\) is continuous at \(x = \pm b\).
  3. For \(\kappa \neq 0\) the family \(p_\kappa(x) = p_0\big(\sqrt{1 - x^2/b^2} + \kappa/\sqrt{1 - x^2/b^2}\big)\) on \(|x| < b\) (with the same \(b\) and \(p_0\), zero outside, the force is then \((1 + 2\kappa)\) times larger) satisfies the slope equation \(g'(x) = 0\) on \((-b, b)\) but not the contact conditions: for \(\kappa > 0\) we have \(g(x) = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\big(G(t) - \kappa\ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\big) < 0\) for \(t > 1\) close to \(1\), for \(\kappa < 0\) we have \(p_\kappa < 0\) for \(1 - t^2 < -\kappa\).
Idea

We show that the inserted pressure makes the gap constant in the contact strip, then we compute the gap outside with the same lemma. The width \(b\) is determined by equating the force and the slope. The edge separates the solution from the remaining ones through the requirement that the gap does not penetrate and the pressure does not pull.

Proof
  1. Slope. For \(|x| < b\) lemma 25.22 gives \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\,\mathrm{PV}\!\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{p(s)}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s = -\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\,\mathrm{PV}\!\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s\), because \(p(s) = (p_0/b)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\). By lemma 25.23 this is \(-\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\,\pi x = -\dfrac{2p_0\,x}{E^* b}\).
  2. Gap in the strip. The derivative of (25.19) is \(g'(x) = x/R + w'(x) = x\big(1/R - 2p_0/(E^* b)\big)\). This is zero for every \(|x| < b\) exactly when \(p_0 = E^* b/(2R)\), which is the second equality in (25.20). The function \(g\) is constant on \([-b, b]\), because it is continuous and has zero derivative. With a suitable choice of \(\delta\) (the constant \(C_0\) in (25.16) and \(\delta\) appear only in the sum \(C_0 - \delta\)) this constant is zero, \(g = 0\) on \(\Omega = [-b, b]\).
  3. Check. We obtained the derivative \(w'\) in step 1 from claim 2 of lemma 25.22, which is stated without proof. So we check the integral of the displacement itself: \(J(x) = \int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\ln|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}s\) must by step 1 have the difference \(J(x) - J(0) = \pi x^2/2\). For \(b = 1\) we get (NumPy) \(0{,}14137\), \(0{,}56549\), \(1{,}27235\) at \(x = 0{,}3, 0{,}6, 0{,}9\), and \(\pi x^2/2\) is equal to five places (num-05.py, part G). By (25.16) we have therefore \(w(x) - w(0) = -\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\cdot\dfrac{\pi x^2}{2} = -\dfrac{p_0\,x^2}{E^* b}\), which is \(-x^2/(2R)\) for \(p_0 = E^* b/(2R)\).
  4. Force. With \(s = b t\) we have \(\int p\,\mathrm{d}s = p_0 b\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1 - t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t = p_0 b\,\pi/2\) (half the area of a circle, numerically also \(1{,}5707963\)). Equating with \(F'\) gives \(p_0 = 2F'/(\pi b)\). By step 2 \(p_0 = E^* b/(2R)\), so \(E^* b/(2R) = 2F'/(\pi b)\) and \(b^2 = 4F'R/(\pi E^*)\). The remaining expression \(p_0 = \sqrt{F'E^*/(\pi R)}\) follows by inserting \(b\) in \(E^*b/(2R)\).
  5. Outside. For \(x > b\), by lemma 25.22, claim 1, and the second value in (25.18), \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\,\pi\big(x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}\big) = -\dfrac{x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}{R}\), with the same \(p_0 = E^*b/(2R)\). Therefore \(g'(x) = \dfrac{x}{R} + w'(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}{R}\).
  6. Since \(w\) is continuous (an integral with an integrable kernel) and \(g(b) = 0\) from step 2, we have \(g(x) = \int_{\mathrm{b}}^x\dfrac{\sqrt{s^2 - b^2}}{R}\,\mathrm{d}s = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\int_1^t\sqrt{\tau^2 - 1}\,\mathrm{d}\tau\) with \(s = b\tau\). The derivative \(G'(t) = \tfrac12\big(\sqrt{t^2 - 1} + t^2/\sqrt{t^2 - 1} - 1/\sqrt{t^2 - 1}\big) = \sqrt{t^2 - 1}\), because \(\dfrac{1 + t/\sqrt{t^2 - 1}}{t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{t^2 - 1}}\), and \(G(1) = 0\). So \(g = (b^2/R)\,G(t)\). Since \(G' > 0\) for \(t > 1\), \(G > 0\) there. For \(x < -b\) the same by evenness. This is claim 2.
  7. Contact conditions. Condition 1 (gap) is satisfied in the strip (\(g = 0\)) and outside (\(g > 0\)). Condition 2 (\(p \geq 0\)) holds because the root is nonnegative. Condition 3 is satisfied because \(p = 0\) where \(g > 0\), and \(g = 0\) where \(p > 0\). Condition 4 is step 4. This is claim 1.
  8. The family. The term \(\kappa p_0/\sqrt{1 - s^2/b^2} = \kappa p_0 b/\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\) gives zero in the slope by the first value in (25.17), so the same \(b, p_0\) keep \(g' = 0\) on \((-b, b)\). Outside, by the first value in (25.18), it adds \(-\dfrac{2\kappa p_0 b}{E^*}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}} = -\dfrac{\kappa b^2}{R\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}\) to \(w'\). Therefore \(g'(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}{R} - \dfrac{\kappa b^2}{R\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}\), and with \(x = b t\) we get \(g = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\big(G(t) - \kappa\ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\big)\) by \(\int_1^t\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\tau^2 - 1}}\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\). As \(t \to 1^+\) we have \(G = O\big((t - 1)^{3/2}\big)\), while the logarithm is \(\sim\sqrt{2(t - 1)}\), so for \(\kappa > 0\) the value of \(g\) near the edge is negative. For \(\kappa < 0\) we have \(\sqrt{1 - t^2} + \kappa/\sqrt{1 - t^2} < 0\) exactly when \(1 - t^2 < -\kappa\).

Source: BARBER §12.5.3 (PDF pp. 195-196): the same \(p(x) = -2F\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}/(\pi a^2)\) (12.60) with the edge from the requirement that the pressure is not singular at \(x = \pm a\) (12.56) (BARBER computes with a pressure of negative sign and a rigid cylinder, and calls the half-width \(a\)). HK (6.50), (6.51) (PDF p. 132): \(\sigma = \frac{2Q}{\pi l b}\big[1 - (y/b)^2\big]^{1/2}\) and \(b\) in the same form (after converting the symbols, \(4Q/(\pi l\,\Sigma\rho)\cdot 1/E^*\)). The proof of claim 3 and of the outside gap is mine. The fact that \(p_\kappa\) covers all solutions of the slope equation is classical (BARBER §12.5, PDF pp. 191-193, Fourier series, and Muskhelishvili, whom BARBER cites in a footnote on p. 192) and we do not prove it, so we do not claim uniqueness of the contact problem.

The meaning of the theorem is easiest to see in a figure.

Let us draw figure 25.17. At the top there is the axis \(x\) and an axis for the pressure. On the contact strip from \(-b\) to \(b\) the pressure is half an ellipse with the largest value \(p_0\) in the middle and zero at the edges. Below it is the second axis, on which we measure the gap downwards. The dashed parabola is the gap of the undeformed bodies \(x^2/(2R)\), which the cylinders would have if they were rigid. The orange curve is the gap under load: in the strip it is zero, outside it is positive, at the edge it grows with the power \(3/2\), as \(G(t) \sim (t - 1)^{3/2}\) shows, and it is everywhere smaller than the parabola. This is the difference between elastic and rigid bodies: under the pressure the bodies are compressed and the gap next to the strip closes.

Let us test the theorem on numbers. For a roller \(R_1 = 5\) mm on a raceway \(R_2 = 25\) mm of the book's steel, \(E^* = 107{,}692\) GPa and \(R = 4{,}1667\) mm. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm the theorem gives \(b = 70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(p_0 = 907{,}0\) MPa, at \(F' = 400\) N/mm \(b = 140{,}37\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(p_0 = 1814{,}1\) MPa (num-05.py, part D). Four times the force gives twice the width and twice the pressure, because \(b\) and \(p_0\) grow as \(\sqrt{F'}\). So the contact is not linear: twice the force does not give twice the pressure. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm we have \(b^2/R = 1{,}182\ \mu\text{m}\). The gap at \(t = 2\), that is \(140\ \mu\text{m}\) from the centre, is \(G(2)\,b^2/R = 1{,}0736\cdot 1{,}182 = 1{,}269\ \mu\text{m}\), while the undeformed gap is \(x^2/(2R) = 2{,}365\ \mu\text{m}\). The two elastic displacements therefore reduce the gap by a little less than half.

Does HK have the same result?
