His equation (6.51) has the same form \(b = [4Q/(\pi l\,\Sigma\rho)\cdot(\ldots)]^{1/2}\), and for steel his (6.52) gives \(b = 3{,}35\cdot 10^{-3}\sqrt{Q/(l\,\Sigma\rho)}\) (mm, N, 1/mm). For our numbers (\(Q/l = 100\) N/mm, \(\Sigma\rho = 0{,}24\) mm\(^{-1}\)) this is \(68{,}4\ \mu\text{m}\), while we got \(70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\). The difference of \(2{,}6\ \%\) is a difference of moduli: from (6.51) and (6.52) at \(\nu = 0{,}3\) it follows that the constant corresponds to \(E = 2{,}065\cdot 10^5\) MPa, while we took \(E = 196\) GPa. The ratio of the roots \(\sqrt{2{,}065/1{,}96} = 1{,}026\) gives \(68{,}4\cdot 1{,}026 = 70{,}2\ \mu\text{m}\), which agrees.

Our two numbers are a measure for the question whether the model still holds. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm we have \(p_0/E^* = 0{,}0084\), at \(400\) N/mm \(0{,}0168\), which is the order of magnitude of the strain under the strip. Section 25.4 took strains below \(10^{-3}\) for the linear theory, so here we are above this limit and the result holds only as far as the steel still behaves as linearly elastic. This limits the model, it does not refute it. The steel of the book has the yield stress (definition 2.7) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa (chapter 3), while our \(p_0 = 907\) MPa is four times larger. For the ball, section 25.6 (lemma 25.29) shows that the steel of the book starts to yield already at \(p_0 = 1{,}613\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 355\) MPa. The stresses below the surface of a line contact we do not compute here (HK §6.4, PDF pp. 133-138), so we do not give the yield limit for the cylinders and do not claim that the steel of the book stays elastic at our forces. The numbers of this section hold for a steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\) that does not yet yield at such a pressure.

The theorem chose one shape of the pressure, the half-ellipse. Would another shape also give zero gap in the strip? Claim 3 says there is a whole family of them, but all except one violate the contact conditions at the edge. This is the near miss of the theorem: a solution of the slope equation is not yet a solution of the contact problem.

Let us draw figure 25.18. On the left is the pressure from \(t = 0{,}6\) to the edge, which is the vertical dashed line at \(b\). The blue curve is \(\kappa = 0\) and falls to zero at \(b\), as in the theorem. The orange one has \(\kappa = 0{,}3\): at the edge it does not fall to zero but grows beyond every bound, and at \(0{,}99\,b\) it is \(2{,}27\,p_0\), at \(0{,}999\,b\) it is \(6{,}75\,p_0\). The grey one has \(\kappa = -0{,}3\) and goes to \(-\infty\) at the edge: at \(0{,}99\,b\) it is \(-1{,}99\,p_0\) and at \(0{,}999\,b\) it is \(-6{,}67\,p_0\), so the contact pulls, which condition 2 forbids. On the right is the gap outside the strip, drawn above the second axis, which starts at the edge of the strip \(t = 1\). For \(\kappa = 0\) (blue) it is positive. For \(\kappa = 0{,}3\) (orange) the gap near the edge is negative, at least \(-0{,}1065\,b^2/R = -126\) nm at \(t = 1{,}14\), and positive only from \(t = 1{,}41\): the bodies would penetrate each other, which condition 1 forbids. For \(\kappa = -0{,}3\) (grey) the gap is positive, but this is reached with a pressure that pulls. Conditions 1 and 2 together therefore leave only \(\kappa = 0\), and this is what BARBER says in words, that the pressure at the edge is not singular: \(\kappa \neq 0\) has a singular pressure at the edge.

The family therefore has two possibilities at the edge, and each violates one of the conditions: for \(\kappa > 0\) the bodies penetrate, for \(\kappa < 0\) the contact pulls. Uniqueness of the contact problem as a whole is not proved by this: we showed that among the family \(p_\kappa\) only the theorem satisfies the contact conditions. That the family covers all solutions of the slope equation is stated by BARBER (see the source of the theorem), we do not prove it. Uniqueness of the contact problem is unproved also in chapter 11 (section 11.7.6), and here too we state it as open.

The proof of the theorem gave the pressure, the width and the gap, but not the approach \(\delta\) of the bodies. This is not a defect of the proof, it is a property of the plane problem.

Lemma 25.25 The approach of a line contact is not defined (približevanje pri črtnem stiku ni določeno)

Let \(p\) be from theorem 25.24 and \(L > b\). Let \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(x)\) be the deflection from lemma 25.22 with the choice \(C_0 = \dfrac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\ln L\), that is \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(x) = \dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}p(s)\,\ln\dfrac{L}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}s\). This is the deflection relative to the point at the distance \(L\) from the middle of the contact, which for \(L \gg b\) approximately stays at rest, since there \(\ln\big(L/|L - s|\big) \approx s/L\) and \(\int p\,s\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) by the evenness of \(p\). Then the deflection under the middle of the strip is

\[w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = \frac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\Big(\ln\frac{2L}{b} + \frac12\Big) , \tag{25.21}\]

and as \(L \to \infty\) it grows beyond every bound, like \(\ln L\). Therefore the distance between the bodies that the contact requires is not determined by \(F'\), \(E^*\) and \(R\) alone, but also by \(L\).

Proof

We must show the value of the integral \(\int p\,\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s\) and think about \(L\).

  1. By definition \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = \dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\Big(F'\ln L - \int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}p(s)\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s\Big)\), because \(\int p = F'\).
  2. With \(s = b u\) and \(p = p_0\sqrt{1 - u^2}\) we have \(\int p\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s = p_0 b\Big(\ln b\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1 - u^2}\,\mathrm{d}u + \int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1 - u^2}\ln|u|\,\mathrm{d}u\Big)\). The first integral is \(\pi/2\). The second is \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\big(\ln\tfrac12 - \tfrac12\big)\) (numerically \(-1{,}8741912\) against \(-1{,}8741912\), num-05.py, part G). Since \(p_0 b\,\pi/2 = F'\), we get \(\int p\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s = F'\big(\ln\tfrac{b}{2} - \tfrac12\big)\).
  3. We insert into step 1: \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = \dfrac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\big(\ln L - \ln\tfrac b2 + \tfrac12\big)\), which is (25.21).

Source: The computation is mine. BARBER §12.4 (PDF p. 190): the deflection is logarithmically unbounded, and the rigid-body displacement of the loaded region relative to distant parts of the body cannot be found without taking the finite size of the body into account.

Let us look at this on numbers. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm we have \(2F'/(\pi E^*) = 0{,}5911\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(b = 70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\). For \(L = 0{,}1\) m we get \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = 4{,}998\ \mu\text{m}\), for \(L = 1\) m \(6{,}359\ \mu\text{m}\). The same bodies therefore "approach" by \(5{,}0\) or by \(6{,}4\ \mu\text{m}\), depending on where on the bodies we measure the distance, and the difference of \(1{,}361\ \mu\text{m}\) is larger than \(b^2/R = 1{,}182\ \mu\text{m}\), which is the scale of everything that happens in the strip (figure 25.17). For the ball (section 25.6) this does not happen, because the deflection \(1/r\) of section 25.4 falls with distance and distant points stay at rest. A logarithm in the plane grows and does not allow anything to stay at rest. For a real cylinder the scale of the body is the length \(l\) of the cylinder, and indeed the Lundberg and Sjövall deflection of a line contact (HK (6.53), PDF pp. 132-133) has in front of the logarithm a factor proportional to \(Q/l\) and in the logarithm the length of the cylinder squared, \(\ln\big(\pi E l^2/(Q\cdots)\big)\). We do not copy the symbols that HK does not explain on this page, and we do not claim agreement with the lemma. The fact is that for roller bearings HK uses the force-approach law \(Q \propto \delta^{n}\) with \(n = 10/9\), not \(3/2\) as for balls (HK (7.3), PDF pp. 155-156). This law is empirical: it comes from the equation \(\delta \propto Q^{0{,}9}/l^{0{,}8}\) (HK (6.54), PDF p. 133), which Palmgren obtained from tests of rollers slightly convex along their length (crowned rollers) loaded against raceways, and \(1/0{,}9 = 10/9\). Whether this is because of what was described, HK does not say. We do not derive the law with \(10/9\) in the book, we quote it as HK.

For a line contact we therefore have the pressure, the width of the strip (\(b \propto \sqrt{F'}\)) and the gap, but the model does not give the approach. Section 25.6 does the same for a sphere, and there the approach exists, because the deflection falls with distance.

Notation and what is left out. Notation of the section: \(b\) is the half-width of the contact, not the radius of a tube from chapter 11. The letter \(\delta\) is the approach of the bodies, not a virtual increment. The letter \(p\) is the pressure in N/m\(^2\), and the force per unit length of the axis is \(F'\) in N/m. Outside the chapter: the ends of cylinders and the crowning of rollers that prevents edge loading (HK, PDF pp. 145-148) are not part of this section, and neither is friction in the contact (HK §6.5, PDF pp. 139-142).

25.6 Hertz contact of a sphere: point contact and elliptical contact

A ball of diameter \(12{,}7\) mm lies on a steel plate and the shaft presses it with a force of \(1000\) N. In section 25.4 we saw that a point force on a half-space gives an infinite deflection and an infinite pressure, so contact at a single point is a model that fails. A real ball and a real plate squeeze together over a small circle. How large is this circle, by how much do the ball and plate approach each other, and what is the pressure in it? We need all three numbers, because in the next sections we build the stiffness of a bearing from them. Since all contacts in a ball bearing are point contacts, we treat them first: a sphere against a plane or another sphere, then a sphere in the groove of a raceway, which is elliptical.

The model has several simplifications, which we name so that they do not slip out of sight. The bodies are homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic (theorem 3.11), with no friction on the contact surface. Near the contact we replace each body by the half-space of section 25.4, which holds if the contact region is much smaller than the dimensions of the bodies. This is one of the three properties of a nonconformal contact (nekonformni stik) from definition 25.18, the other two (contact at a point, smooth surfaces) hold for a sphere. Hertz assumed in addition that the load is perpendicular to the surface and that the contact circle is small against the radii of curvature (HK, PDF p. 125). The contact conditions are those of definition 25.19: the gap is nonnegative, the pressure is nonnegative, and at every point at least one of them is zero.

Let us draw figure 25.19, first the left panel. The flat body is the support: its surface is a horizontal line and the steel is below it. On it stands the sphere of radius \(R\) and centre \(C\), which touches the support at the point \(O\). At a distance \(r\) from \(O\) we measure horizontally, which the dimension \(r\) shows. The sphere moves away from the support with distance, the gap \(g_0(r)\) between them is shaded in the figure. We compute it from the right triangle with sides \(R - g_0\) and \(r\) and hypotenuse \(R\): \((R - g_0)^2 + r^2 = R^2\), hence \(g_0 = R - \sqrt{R^2 - r^2}\). Since \(r\) in the contact is much smaller than \(R\), \(\sqrt{R^2 - r^2} \approx R - r^2/(2R)\) and

\[g_0(r) \approx \frac{r^2}{2R} . \tag{25.22}\]

This parabola is accurate enough for the contact. At a force of \(1000\) N, when \(a = 353{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\) (result below), the true gap at the edge of the contact is \(9{,}8545\ \mu\text{m}\) and the parabola gives \(9{,}8468\ \mu\text{m}\), which is \(0{,}078\ \%\) less (NumPy, num-06.py). Why we need this number at all: the contact condition requires the gap to be exactly zero, and we must therefore know it precisely, not only roughly.

What happens when we press? The right panel shows the support after loading: under the pressure it yields and in the circle it increases its distance from the far plane. The sphere is also flattened at the bottom. In the contact circle of radius \(a\) the two surfaces are the same curve, outside it the gap opens again. The force \(F\) acts along the axis and ends at the sphere, because it pushes it. The centre of the sphere has moved from its initial position by the approach \(h\) (približevanje), which the dimension \(h\) shows. We measure it against points far from the contact, because the deflection of a half-space decays as \(1/r\) (corollary 25.16), so for \(r \gg a\) there is no displacement left.

With two bodies we have two ingredients. The first is the gap: if the bodies have radii \(R_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\), the gap is the sum of the gaps, \(g_0 = r^2/(2R_{\mathrm{A}}) + r^2/(2R_{\mathrm{B}}) = r^2/(2R)\) with the radius \(R\) given by

\[\frac1R = \frac1{R_{\mathrm{A}}} + \frac1{R_{\mathrm{B}}} . \tag{25.23}\]

A plane is \(R_{\mathrm{B}} \to \infty\). The second is the modulus. Both bodies receive the same pressure \(p\) (by Newton's third law the forces of opposite directions are equal), each yields as a half-space, and by lemma 25.17 the deflections \(w_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{B}}\) add. For each body \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \dfrac{1 - \nu_{\mathrm{i}}^2}{\pi E_{\mathrm{i}}}\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A\), so the total indentation is

\[u(x) = w_{\mathrm{A}} + w_{\mathrm{B}} = \frac{1}{\pi E^*}\int_{\mathrm{A}} \frac{p(s)}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}A(s) , \qquad \frac1{E^*} = \frac{1 - \nu_{\mathrm{A}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{A}}} + \frac{1 - \nu_{\mathrm{B}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{B}}} . \tag{25.24}\]

This is the effective modulus (učinkoviti modul) \(E^*\) as BOWER writes it (PDF p. 331) and as section 25.5 has it for cylinders, here expressed with two fractions (its form \(E_{\mathrm{A}} E_{\mathrm{B}}/((1 - \nu_{\mathrm{A}}^2)E_{\mathrm{B}} + (1 - \nu_{\mathrm{B}}^2)E_{\mathrm{A}})\) is the same). The letter \(E^*\) is here an italic scalar, different from the bold \(\mat E^*\) of the Euler-Almansi strain in chapter 1. For two equal steel bodies (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\)) \(E^* = E/(2(1 - \nu^2)) = 107{,}692\) GPa, and for a sphere \(D = 12{,}7\) mm on a plane \(R = 6{,}35\) mm, for two such spheres \(R = 3{,}175\) mm. We write the approach \(h\) (BOWER), in the following sections \(\delta\), which is the same quantity. The word Hertz comes from Heinrich Hertz, of whom the history a little below tells.

Before we write the solution, we ask what kind of pressure we expect at all. The gap \(g_0\) is a parabola, so in the contact the indentation \(u\) must have the form \(h - r^2/(2R)\) for the gap to be zero. With the uniform pressure that we computed in section 25.4.1 this does not happen: the deflection is largest at the centre and at the edge it is \(2/\pi\) of the central one. We therefore look for a pressure that gives a parabolic deflection. Hertz took a pressure of the shape of a semi-ellipsoid, and the test is a calculation.

Lemma 25.26 Deflection under a semi-ellipsoidal pressure (poves pod polelipsoidnim tlakom)

Let \(A_{\mathrm{a}}\) be a disc of radius \(a\) centred at \(O\) on the surface of a half-space, let \(p_0 > 0\) and let the pressure be \(p(s) = p_0\sqrt{1 - |s|^2/a^2}\) for \(|s| \leq a\) and zero outside. Let \(u(x) = \dfrac{1}{\pi E^*}\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{a}} \dfrac{p(s)}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}A(s)\) (equation (25.24)) and \(r = |x|\). Then:

  1. \(F = \int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{a}} p\,\mathrm{d}A = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\,p_0\,a^2\),
  2. \(u(0) = \dfrac{\pi\,p_0\,a}{2E^*}\),
  3. for \(r \leq a\), \(u(r) = \dfrac{\pi\,p_0}{4E^*a}\,(2a^2 - r^2)\) (cited, see the source line, and checked numerically),
  4. for \(r > a\), \(u(r) = \dfrac{p_0}{2E^*a}\Big((2a^2 - r^2)\arcsin\dfrac ar + a\sqrt{r^2 - a^2}\Big)\).
Proof

We prove claims 1, 2 and 4, claim 3 is cited. We use polar coordinates (theorem 4.59, \(J = \rho\)), in steps 1 and 2 around the centre, in steps 3 and 4 around the point \(x\) outside the disc.

  1. By the change of variables theorem \(F = p_0\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^a \sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\;s\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}\theta\). With \(t = 1 - s^2/a^2\), \(\int_0^a s\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,\mathrm{d}s = \dfrac{a^2}{2}\int_0^1\sqrt t\,\mathrm{d}t = \dfrac{a^2}{3}\). So \(F = 2\pi p_0 a^2/3\). This is claim 1.
  2. At the centre \(|x - s| = s\) and the factor \(s\) from the Jacobian cancels \(1/s\). Hence \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = p_0\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^a\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 2\pi p_0\cdot\dfrac{\pi a}{4}\), because \(\int_0^a\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,\mathrm{d}s\) is the area of a quarter of a circle of radius \(a\) divided by \(a\), which is \(\pi a/4\). Dividing by \(\pi E^*\) gives claim 2.
  3. Claim 4: the point \(x\) is outside the disc at distance \(r > a\) from the centre. A ray from \(x\) at angle \(\varphi\) from the axis through the centre meets the disc only for \(|\sin\varphi| \leq a/r\), at distances \(\rho_{1,2} = r\cos\varphi \mp \sqrt{a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi}\). A point \(s = x + \rho\,\vek e\) on the ray (with \(\vek e\) the unit vector of the ray) has \(|s|^2 - a^2 = (\rho - \rho_1)(\rho - \rho_2)\), so \(p = (p_0/a)\sqrt{(\rho_2 - \rho)(\rho - \rho_1)}\). In polar coordinates around \(x\), \(J = \rho\) and \(\rho\) cancels \(1/|x - s|\), so \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = \int\!\int p\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\). The inner integral \(\int_{\rho_1}^{\rho_2}(p_0/a)\sqrt{(\rho_2 - \rho)(\rho - \rho_1)}\,\mathrm{d}\rho\) is the area of a half-disc of radius \((\rho_2 - \rho_1)/2\) multiplied by \(p_0/a\), that is \(\dfrac{p_0}{a}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{8}(\rho_2 - \rho_1)^2 = \dfrac{\pi p_0}{2a}(a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi)\), because \(\rho_2 - \rho_1 = 2\sqrt{a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi}\).
  4. Continuation of claim 4. We integrate over \(\varphi\) from \(-\varphi_0\) to \(\varphi_0\) with \(\sin\varphi_0 = a/r\): \(\int_{-\varphi_0}^{\varphi_0}(a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = (2a^2 - r^2)\,\varphi_0 + r^2\sin\varphi_0\cos\varphi_0 = (2a^2 - r^2)\,\varphi_0 + a\sqrt{r^2 - a^2}\), because \(\sin^2\varphi = \tfrac12(1 - \cos 2\varphi)\). Multiplying by \(\pi p_0/(2a)\) and dividing by \(\pi E^*\) is claim 4. At \(r = a\) the formula gives \(\pi p_0 a/(4E^*)\), which is half the value at the centre and equals what claim 3 gives at \(r = a\).

Source: Claims 1 and 2 are a calculation in SymPy (num-06.py B). Claim 4 is our calculation (num-06.py G). Claim 3 is from BOWER (PDF p. 331, the equations for \(a\), \(h\), \(p_0\) that follow from it and that we check below) and HK (PDF pp. 125-129), a proof for points inside the circle is not in the book. We checked it as follows: in polar coordinates around \(x\) the radial integral for \(|x| = r \leq a\) is likewise an area under a half-circle, which gives a one-dimensional integral over \(\varphi\): the ratio \(u(r)\big/\big(\tfrac{\pi p_0}{4E^*a}(2a^2 - r^2)\big)\) equals \(1\) to ten digits at \(r/a = 0\), \(0{,}3\), \(0{,}6\), \(0{,}9\), \(0{,}99\) (num-06.py F).

The proof has four parts, which we read on the figure. The right panel of figure 25.20 has \(r/a\) on the horizontal axis and the indentation and the gap, divided by \(h = u(0)\), on the vertical one. The blue curve is the deflection \(u/h\). Inside the contact it is a parabola from \(1\) to \(\tfrac12\) by claim 3, outside it decays as by claim 4. At \(r = a\) the two branches meet at the same point \(\tfrac12\), which is a check of both claims. For large \(r\) claim 4 goes to \(\dfrac{u}{h} \to \dfrac{4a}{3\pi r}\), so \(u \to \dfrac{F}{\pi E^* r}\) with \(F\) from claim 1: the same \(1/r\) as in corollary 25.16. So a pressure on a circle acts from afar as a point force, which we also saw for uniform pressure in section 25.4.1 with another number.

Uniform pressure would not do. We check that the semi-ellipsoid is not just one of the possibilities. For uniform pressure \(q\) on the same circle, in polar coordinates around a point \(x\) inside the circle, \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = q\int_0^{2\pi}\ell(\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\), where \(\ell(\varphi) = \sqrt{a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi} - r\cos\varphi\) is the distance from \(x\) to the edge of the circle in the direction \(\varphi\). The term \(-r\cos\varphi\) gives zero over a full turn, so the integral equals \(4q\,a\,E(r/a)\) with the complete elliptic integral of the second kind \(E(k) = \int_0^{\pi/2}(1 - k^2\sin^2\varphi)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\) (this \(E\) is not a modulus). So \(u(a)/u(0) = 2/\pi = 0{,}6366\) (this is the ratio of section 25.4.1, the blackwhite dot in the right panel of figure 25.20), while for the semi-ellipsoid it is \(\tfrac12\) (the blue dot). Let the radius \(R\) be chosen so that the gap at the edge matches (\(a^2/(2R) = u(0) - u(a)\)). At half the radius the deflection of uniform pressure is \(u(a/2)/u(0) = 0{,}9342\) and a parabola through both ends would give \(0{,}9092\), so the gap there is \(+0{,}0251\,u(0)\), larger than zero, and in the contact the surfaces would not touch (num-06.py J). For the semi-ellipsoid the fit is exact: \(u(a/2)/u(0) = 0{,}875 = 1 - \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14\).

The contact condition also requires that the pressure is nonnegative everywhere and that the gap outside the contact is larger than zero. The first is satisfied, since the root is nonnegative. For the second we open the left panel of figure 25.20. The surface is a line, the pressure is the semi-ellipse, drawn as arrows that push the body down, and the cylinder of height \(p_0\) on the same circle of diameter \(2a\) is for comparison. The volume of a semi-ellipsoid is two thirds of the cylinder, \(\tfrac23\,p_0\pi a^2\), which is claim 1. The gap in the right panel is the orange curve: outside the contact \(g = \dfrac{r^2}{2R} - h + u(r)\), and with \(h = a^2/R\) (we derive this equality in the proof of the theorem below) and claim 4 at \(r/a = 1{,}1\), \(1{,}3\), \(2\), \(3\) we get \(g/h = 0{,}0378\), \(0{,}196\), \(1{,}218\), \(3{,}643\), so everywhere more than zero.

So we can write the theorem. Its proof is supplemented by a statement of what remains outside the book.

Theorem 25.27 Hertz contact of two spheres (Hertzov stik dveh krogel)

Let two bodies touch at a point, let them have radii \(R_{\mathrm{A}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\) and effective modulus \(E^*\) (equation (25.24)), \(R\) by equation (25.23), let the gap be \(g_0 = r^2/(2R)\) (equation (25.22)) and the force \(F > 0\). If claim 3 of lemma 25.26 holds, the radius of the contact circle \(a\), the approach \(h\) and the maximum pressure \(p_0\) have the values

\[a = \Big(\frac{3FR}{4E^*}\Big)^{1/3} , \qquad h = \frac{a^2}{R} = \Big(\frac{9F^2}{16\,R\,E^{*2}}\Big)^{1/3} , \qquad p_0 = \frac{3F}{2\pi a^2} = \Big(\frac{6F\,E^{*2}}{\pi^3R^2}\Big)^{1/3} , \tag{25.25}\]

the pressure \(p(r) = p_0\sqrt{1 - r^2/a^2}\) for \(r \leq a\) satisfies all contact conditions (definition 25.19) and \(F = \dfrac43\,E^*\sqrt R\;h^{3/2}\).

Proof

We must show that the triple \((a, h, p)\) satisfies all three contact conditions, and express \(a\), \(h\), \(p_0\) from them.

  1. In the contact the gap must be zero: \(g_0(r) + u(r) - h = 0\) for \(r \leq a\). By claim 3 of lemma 25.26 this is \(\dfrac{r^2}{2R} + \dfrac{\pi p_0}{4E^*a}(2a^2 - r^2) - h = 0\).
  2. The coefficient of \(r^2\) must be zero: \(\dfrac1{2R} - \dfrac{\pi p_0}{4E^*a} = 0\), so \(p_0 = \dfrac{2E^*a}{\pi R}\). The constant term must be zero: \(h = \dfrac{\pi p_0 a}{2E^*} = \dfrac{a^2}{R}\) (with \(p_0\) from the previous step). This is the second equality.
  3. By claim 1 of the lemma \(F = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}p_0a^2\). Inserting \(p_0\): \(F = \dfrac{4E^*a^3}{3R}\) and \(a^3 = \dfrac{3FR}{4E^*}\), which is the first equality. The equality \(p_0 = 3F/(2\pi a^2)\) is claim 1 of the lemma, the second expression for \(p_0\) follows from \(p_0^3 = \dfrac{8E^{*3}a^3}{\pi^3R^3} = \dfrac{6FE^{*2}}{\pi^3R^2}\).
  4. Outside the circle the pressure is zero (so nonnegative), and the gap is \(g = \dfrac{r^2}{2R} - h + u(r)\) with \(u\) from claim 4 of the lemma. With \(\rho = r/a > 1\), \(h = a^2/R\) from step 2 and \(\arcsin(1/\rho) = \pi/2 - \arccos(1/\rho)\) we get \(\dfrac gh = \dfrac1\pi\Big((\rho^2 - 2)\arccos\dfrac1\rho + \sqrt{\rho^2 - 1}\Big)\) (SymPy, chk-06.py). For \(\rho \geq \sqrt2\) the first term is nonnegative and the second positive, so \(g > 0\). For \(1 < \rho < \sqrt2\) we write \(\rho = 1/\cos\vartheta\) with \(\vartheta \in (0, \pi/4)\). Then \(\sqrt{\rho^2 - 1} = \tan\vartheta\) and \(\rho^2 - 2 = -\cos 2\vartheta/\cos^2\vartheta\), so \(\pi\cos^2\vartheta\cdot\dfrac gh = \sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta - \vartheta\cos 2\vartheta = \tfrac12\cos 2\vartheta\,(\tan 2\vartheta - 2\vartheta)\). Since \(2\vartheta \in (0, \pi/2)\), \(\cos 2\vartheta > 0\). Also \(\tan x > x\) for \(x \in (0, \pi/2)\), because by theorem 1.84 \(\tan x - x = x\,(1/\cos^2\xi - 1) = x\tan^2\xi > 0\) for some \(\xi \in (0, x)\). Hence \(g > 0\) for every \(r > a\). In numbers: at \(r/a = 1{,}1\), \(1{,}3\), \(2\), \(3\), \(g/h = 0{,}0378\), \(0{,}196\), \(1{,}218\), \(3{,}643\). In the circle \(p \cdot g = 0\) (\(g = 0\)), outside (\(p = 0\)), which is the third condition.
  5. From \(h = a^2/R\) and \(a = (3FR/(4E^*))^{1/3}\), \(h^{3/2} = a^3/R^{3/2} = \dfrac{3F}{4E^*\sqrt R}\), so \(F = \dfrac43E^*\sqrt R\,h^{3/2}\).

Source: BOWER, §5.4.10 (PDF p. 331): the equations for \(a\), \(h\), \(p_0\), checked on the crop (p331-b2, p331-b3). HK (PDF p. 129) the same with general \(a^*\), \(b^*\), \(\delta^*\) (\(a^* = b^* = \delta^* = 1\) for spheres). The proof by steps is a derivation from the lemma, not from a book. We do not prove that the solution is unique (the same reason as for theorem 11.4: the book does not prove it for the contact problem, see the remark in chapter 11), only that the triple satisfies the conditions, given the cited claim 3 of the lemma. Step 4 for \(r > a\) is our proof, not from a book.

We test the Hertz solution on numbers we know. A ball \(D = 12{,}7\) mm on a flat steel plate (\(E^* = 107{,}692\) GPa, \(R = 6{,}35\) mm): at \(F = 100\) N, \(a = 164{,}1\ \mu\text{m}\), \(h = 4{,}24\ \mu\text{m}\), \(p_0 = 1772\) MPa, and at \(F = 1000\) N, \(a = 353{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\), \(h = 19{,}69\ \mu\text{m}\), \(p_0 = 3818\) MPa. A ten times larger force gives a \(10^{1/3} = 2{,}154\) times larger \(a\) and \(p_0\), not ten times. Two such balls (\(R = 3{,}175\) mm) at \(1000\) N: \(a = 280{,}7\ \mu\text{m}\), \(h = 24{,}81\ \mu\text{m}\), \(p_0 = 6061\) MPa, which is more than for the plane, because the curvature is larger and the contact smaller (num-06.py A).

We check the sense of the model with the stated bounds (rule 46). At \(F = 1000\) N, \(a/R = 0{,}056\), so the error of the parabola for the gap is \(a^2/(4R^2) = 7{,}8\cdot 10^{-4}\), which is \(0{,}078\ \%\), and a half-space is a good picture of the bodies. Linearity is different: the strains under the contact are of the order \(p_0/E = 3818/196\,000 = 0{,}019\), which is more than the \(10^{-3}\) that linear theory assumes (section 25.4), and at \(100\) N \(0{,}009\). This error is therefore more than an order of magnitude larger than the error of the gap, and with the warning that follows we add that we take the elastic calculation as an approximation.

Although HK gives its own constants for steel, their values are not in contradiction with ours. HK (6.41) writes for the inner raceway \(b = 0{,}0236\,b^*\,(Q/\Sigma\rho)^{1/3}\) mm and (6.43) \(\delta = 2{,}79\cdot10^{-4}\,\delta^*(Q^2\Sigma\rho)^{1/3}\) mm (PDF p. 129, crop 6.41 and the text of the page, \(Q\) in N, \(\rho\) in mm\(^{-1}\)). For a sphere on a plane \(b^* = a^* = \delta^* = 1\), \(\Sigma\rho = 2/R\) and \(Q = 1000\) N, which gives \(a = 346{,}9\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(\delta = 18{,}98\ \mu\text{m}\) against our \(353{,}6\) and \(19{,}69\ \mu\text{m}\). The difference is explained by the modulus: the constant \(0{,}0236\) corresponds to \(E = 207{,}7\) GPa at \(\nu = 0{,}3\), which is \(6{,}0\ \%\) more than our \(196\) GPa. With this modulus our calculation would give HK's two numbers (num-06.py I).

Corollary 25.28 Contact stiffness (togost stika)

Under the conditions of theorem 25.27 the contact stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}h}\) equals \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = 2E^*a = \dfrac{3F}{2h}\). It grows as \(F^{1/3}\) and goes to zero as \(F \to 0\).

Proof

From theorem 25.27 \(F = K h^{3/2}\) with \(K = \tfrac43E^*\sqrt R\), so by the rule of differentiation \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}h} = \tfrac32 K h^{1/2} = \dfrac{3F}{2h}\). With \(h = a^2/R\), \(K h^{1/2} = \tfrac43E^*\sqrt R\cdot a/\sqrt R = \tfrac43E^*a\), so \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}h} = 2E^*a\). Because \(a \propto F^{1/3}\) (equation (25.25)), \(k_{\mathrm{c}} \propto F^{1/3}\) and \(a \to 0\) as \(F \to 0\).

Source: BOWER, §5.4.10 (PDF pp. 331-332): \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = 2E^*a\), for every axisymmetric contact with radius \(a\). The proof for a sphere is the differentiation of the theorem.

Let us draw this on figure 25.21. Horizontally is the approach \(h\) in \(\mu\)m, vertically the force \(F\) in N. The blue curve is \(F = K h^{3/2}\). The orange tangent at \(100\) N has the slope \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = 35{,}35\) N/\(\mu\)m, the tangent at \(1000\) N \(76{,}17\) N/\(\mu\)m, which is \(2{,}154\) times more. If the contact were a linear spring, the curve would be the dashed straight line through the origin and \(1000\) N with the stiffness \(F/h = 50{,}8\) N/\(\mu\)m. The curve is below it, because the contact area grows with load and the contact stiffens (hardening, otrdi), which is the reason the Hertz contact is a nonlinear spring. At zero force the tangent is horizontal: an unloaded contact has zero stiffness, which we will need in section 25.8 as a critical point.

Under the ball. Until now we looked at the surface. For a bearing we are also interested in what happens in the interior, because that is where the steel begins to yield. We have the answer from the point force: we cut the pressure into rings and add the stresses of the Boussinesq solution over the rings.

Lemma 25.29 Stresses on the axis of the contact (napetosti na osi stika)

Under the conditions of theorem 25.27 and for \(z \geq 0\) the stresses on the axis under the centre of the contact are principal and:

  1. \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}(z) = -\dfrac{p_0}{1 + z^2/a^2}\) (proved),
  2. \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}(z) = \sigma_\theta(z) = -p_0\Big((1 + \nu)\Big(1 - \dfrac za\arctan\dfrac az\Big) - \dfrac{1}{2(1 + z^2/a^2)}\Big)\) (cited, checked numerically),
  3. the largest shear stress on the axis is \(\tau_{\max} = 0{,}310\,p_0\) at \(z = 0{,}481\,a\) for \(\nu = 0{,}3\), and the von Mises stress there is \(0{,}620\,p_0\).
Proof
  1. We cut the pressure into rings: a point on the axis at depth \(z\) is at distance \(R = \sqrt{s^2 + z^2}\) from a point of a ring of radius \(s\). By theorem 25.15 the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of a point force is \(-3Fz^3/(2\pi R^5)\), so by superposition (lemma 25.17, Riemann sums of rings, which theorem 4.59 sends to an integral) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}(z) = -\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^a\dfrac{3z^3}{2\pi R^5}\,p_0\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\;s\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -3z^3p_0\int_0^a\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,s}{(s^2 + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. With \(t = s^2/a^2\) and \(a = 1\) (units), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} = -\tfrac32\,p_0z^3\int_0^1\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\mathrm{d}t\). The function \(G(t) = (1 - t)^{3/2}(t + z^2)^{-3/2}\) has the derivative \(G'(t) = -\tfrac32\,\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\big((t + z^2) + (1 - t)\big) = -\tfrac32(1 + z^2)\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}}\) (SymPy, checked at three points).
  3. Hence \(\int_0^1\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\mathrm{d}t = -\dfrac{2}{3(1 + z^2)}\big(G(1) - G(0)\big) = \dfrac{2}{3(1 + z^2)\,z^3}\), because \(G(1) = 0\) and \(G(0) = z^{-3}\). Inserting: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} = -\dfrac{p_0}{1 + z^2}\). This is claim 1.
  4. Claim 2: we get the radial stress by the same summation from the Boussinesq \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). We quote the formula for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\) from BOWER (PDF p. 332) and check it: the sum over rings with \(4000\) terms gives at \(z/a = 0{,}1\), \(0{,}48\), \(1\), \(2\) the values \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}/p_0 = -0{,}99010\), \(-0{,}81274\), \(-0{,}50000\), \(-0{,}20000\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}/p_0 = -0{,}61370\), \(-0{,}19270\), \(-0{,}02898\), \(+0{,}00548\), which equals the two formulas to five digits (num-06.py D).
  5. On the axis, by axial symmetry, \(\sigma_\theta = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{zr}} = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\sigma_\theta\) are principal stresses (definition 2.60). By theorem 2.70 \(\tau_{\max} = |\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}|/2\) and the von Mises stress (definition 2.76) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}} = \sigma_\theta\) equals \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}| = 2\tau_{\max}\). We compute the difference \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}|/2\) by claims 1 and 2 (\(\nu = 0{,}3\)) at \(30\,000\) points and get the largest value \(0{,}3100\,p_0\) at \(z = 0{,}481\,a\). There \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}8122\,p_0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}} = -0{,}1922\,p_0\).

Source: BOWER, §5.4.10 (PDF pp. 332-333): \(\sigma_{33}\) and \(\sigma_{11} = \sigma_{22}\) on the axis (crop p332-b3), the largest von Mises \(0{,}6200\) at \(0{,}481\,a\). HK (PDF p. 136) reads from a graph \(0{,}467\) at the largest shear, which is \(3\ \%\) less, and we do not know which Poisson ratio it took. Claim 1 is a proof and is not in the sources in this form, claim 2 is cited and checked.

Let us look at this on figure 25.22. On the left is the depth \(z/a\) vertically and the stress in units of \(p_0\) horizontally. The orange curve is \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}\) and at the surface it is \(1\): there the pressure equals \(p_0\), and at depth \(a\) only \(\tfrac12\). The grey curve is \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\) and at the surface it is \(0{,}8\,p_0\), because \((1 + 2\nu)/2 = 0{,}8\). For the shear stress we take the difference, the blue curve has only \(0{,}1\,p_0\) at the surface and reaches its maximum \(0{,}310\,p_0\) deep below the surface. What does this mean? The largest load is under the contact, not in it. On the right this is drawn in true proportions: the contact is the wide line of width \(2a\), the point is on the axis \(z\) at depth \(0{,}481\,a\), which at \(F = 1000\) N is \(0{,}481\cdot 353{,}6 = 170\ \mu\text{m}\).

Outside the elastic range. Steel begins to yield at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (definition 2.7) and the book takes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa for steel (chapter 11, BOWER Table 3.9, PDF p. 156). By claim 3 of the lemma this happens at \(0{,}620\,p_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\), so \(p_0 = 1{,}613\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 354{,}8\) MPa. With \(p_0 \propto F^{1/3}\) (equation (25.25)) this means \(F_{\mathrm{Y}} = 0{,}80\) N for a ball \(D = 12{,}7\) mm, at a contact radius of \(32{,}9\ \mu\text{m}\) and a depth of \(15{,}8\ \mu\text{m}\).

Let us compare with the earlier values. At \(100\) N and \(1000\) N \(p_0/\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 8{,}05\) and \(17{,}35\), so the Hertz result in these contacts is not usable for the book's mild steel: the steel yields long before. Figure 25.23 shows this.

Both axes have a logarithmic scale, the horizontal one for the force \(F\) in N, the vertical one for the pressure \(p_0\) in MPa. The blue straight line is \(p_0 \propto F^{1/3}\) (slope \(\tfrac13\)). The orange line is the limit \(1{,}613\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) and the straight line crosses it at \(F_{\mathrm{Y}} = 0{,}80\) N, in the orange point with the vertical. The points for \(100\) N and \(1000\) N are the blue points, far above the limit. What does a bearing do? Rolling bearings have rings and balls of steel hardened to \(61\) to \(65\) Rockwell C (HK, PDF pp. 22-23), and HK (PDF p. 121) writes that bearings run continuously at normal stresses above \(1380\) MPa and in tests above \(3449\) MPa. Both values are the dotted lines in the figure. For this hardened steel the yield stress is much higher than the book's \(220\) MPa, but we do not quote it here because it is not in our sources. The Hertz calculation remains usable for hardened steel if we take its yield stress.

From history

Heinrich Rudolf Hertz (1857-1894) was born in Hamburg and in 1877 entered the polytechnic institute in Munich, but soon moved to Berlin to Helmholtz and Kirchhoff (TIMO, PDF p. 286). In the autumn of 1880 he became Helmholtz's assistant, and when working with Newton's coloured rings he became interested in the theory of compression of elastic bodies (TIMO, PDF p. 287). In January 1881 he presented a paper on it to the Physical Society in Berlin. In it he gave the general solution of the problem, applied it to particular cases and prepared a numerical table that simplified its use, and extended the theory to impact and derived formulas for the duration of impact of two spheres and for the stresses during it (TIMO, PDF p. 287). The paper interested engineers too, so at their request he prepared a second version, in which he described experiments with compression of glass bodies and circular cylinders. One of the bodies he covered with a thin layer of soot before compression, and as the outline of the contact surface he obtained an ellipse whose axes he could measure accurately, which was an experimental proof of the theory (TIMO, PDF p. 287). The year 1881 is by LOVE (PDF p. 212, footnote) and TIMO (PDF p. 287, footnote): Crelle, J. reine angew. Math. 92. HK (PDF p. 121) writes that the classical solution was established by Hertz in 1896, but that is the year of the reprint of his collected works, not the year of the result.

Let us return to the ellipse that Hertz saw in the soot: the contact of two bodies that are not both spheres cannot be described by one radius, so we need a more general description of curvature. We begin with the groove in the raceway, where the ball rolls.

We start with the left panel of figure 25.24. The ball has radius \(r_{\mathrm{b}} = 6{,}35\) mm and in the figure it is cut perpendicular to the rolling direction. The raceway has a groove with an arc of radius \(r_{\mathrm{g}}\) a little larger than \(r_{\mathrm{b}}\), because the ball must fit into it, and the radii \(r_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(r_{\mathrm{g}}\) are drawn from their centres. In the transverse plane the ball therefore has curvature \(1/r_{\mathrm{b}}\) and the groove \(-1/r_{\mathrm{g}}\) (negative, because it is concave), and in the rolling plane the ball has \(1/r_{\mathrm{b}}\) and the raceway of radius \(25\) mm \(+1/25\) mm\(^{-1}\). We need a rule that adds the curvatures.

Definition 25.30 Curvature sum and difference (vsota in razlika ukrivljenosti)

Let two bodies touch at a point \(O\) and let each of them have at \(O\) a smooth surface with curvatures \(\rho = 1/r\) in two perpendicular planes (\(x\), \(y\), principal planes), positive for a convex and negative for a concave surface (HK, PDF p. 69). Let the principal planes of both bodies coincide. Denote by \(\rho_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\rho_{\mathrm{y}}\) the sums of the curvatures of both bodies in the plane \(x\) and in the plane \(y\), where \(\rho_{\mathrm{x}} \leq \rho_{\mathrm{y}}\) and both are positive. The gap before loading is \(g_0(x, y) = A\,x^2 + B\,y^2\) with \(A = \rho_{\mathrm{x}}/2\) and \(B = \rho_{\mathrm{y}}/2\). The curvature sum (\(\Sigma\rho\)) is \(\Sigma\rho = \rho_{\mathrm{x}} + \rho_{\mathrm{y}}\) and the curvature difference is \(\Phi = (\rho_{\mathrm{y}} - \rho_{\mathrm{x}})/\Sigma\rho\), a number between \(0\) and \(1\). The principal relative radii are \(R_1 = 1/\rho_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(R_2 = 1/\rho_{\mathrm{x}}\) (\(R_1 \leq R_2\)), the effective radius \(R_{\mathrm{e}} = \sqrt{R_1R_2}\).

The letter \(\Phi\) is here the curvature difference, HK writes it \(F(\rho)\) (equation 2.26, PDF p. 70), which would be confused with the force. The same holds for \(A\) and \(B\) here: BOWER (PDF p. 333) writes with \(A\) and \(B\) the sum and the difference, we have them as the coefficients of the gap, the sum and difference are \(\Sigma\rho\) and \(\Sigma\rho\,\Phi\). If \(\Phi = 0\) the contact is a circle (a sphere on a sphere or a plane), if \(\Phi \to 1\) the contact is very elongated: the curvature in one direction \(\rho_{\mathrm{x}} \to 0\), such is the contact of a cylinder (HK, PDF p. 70).

In our case in the rolling plane \(\rho_{\mathrm{y}} = 1/r_{\mathrm{b}} + 1/25 = 0{,}1975\) mm\(^{-1}\) and in the transverse plane \(\rho_{\mathrm{x}} = 1/r_{\mathrm{b}} - 1/r_{\mathrm{g}} = 0{,}0061\) mm\(^{-1}\) (\(r_{\mathrm{g}} = 0{,}52\cdot 12{,}7\) mm), so \(\Sigma\rho = 0{,}20354\) mm\(^{-1}\), \(\Phi = 0{,}9405\), \(R_1 = 5{,}064\) mm, \(R_2 = 165{,}10\) mm, \(R_2/R_1 = 32{,}60\) (num-06.py E). The transverse radius of curvature is thus almost equal to the radius of the ball, which is the measure that HK (PDF p. 64) calls osculation (\(\phi = D/(2r) = 1/(2f)\)): in our case \(1/(2\cdot 0{,}52) = 0{,}96\), so close to \(1\).

The contact is no longer a circle. In the right panel of figure 25.24 is the orange ellipse with semi-axes \(a = 728\ \mu\text{m}\) along the transverse direction \(x\) (\(x\) is the horizontal axis) and \(b = 78{,}0\ \mu\text{m}\) along the rolling (\(y\)). The longer axis is in the direction in which the surfaces separate less, because the gap \(A x^2 + B y^2\) grows more slowly along \(x\) (\(A < B\)). The dashed circle is the contact of a ball on a plane at the same force: the length of the ellipse is \(4{,}4\) times the radius of the circle, and the area is \(0{,}1786\) mm\(^2\) against \(0{,}0846\) mm\(^2\), so \(2{,}1\) times larger, and therefore the pressure at the centre is \(840\) MPa against \(1772\) MPa.

The ellipse, which Hertz could show only with soot, we do not derive in the book but cite.

Theorem 25.31 Hertz elliptical contact (Hertzov eliptični stik)

Let two bodies touch by definition 25.30 with the gap \(g_0 = x^2/(2R_2) + y^2/(2R_1)\) and let the Hertz assumption from the beginning of the section hold. Let \(e \in [0, 1)\) be the solution of the equation

\[\frac{R_2}{R_1} = \frac{K(e) - E(e)/(1 - e^2)}{E(e) - K(e)} , \tag{25.26}\]

where \(K\) and \(E\) are the complete elliptic integrals of the first and second kind (\(K(e) = \int_0^{\pi/2}(1 - e^2\sin^2\varphi)^{-1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\), \(E(e) = \int_0^{\pi/2}(1 - e^2\sin^2\varphi)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\)). The contact surface is an ellipse with the area

\[A = \pi a b = \pi\Big(\frac{3FR_{\mathrm{e}}}{\pi E^*}\Big)^{2/3}\Big(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\Big)^{1/3}\frac{\sqrt{1 - e^2}}{e^{4/3}}\,\big(K(e) - E(e)\big)^{2/3} , \tag{25.27}\]

with semi-axes \(a = \sqrt{A/\pi}\,(1 - e^2)^{-1/4}\) along \(x\) and \(b = \sqrt{A/\pi}\,(1 - e^2)^{1/4}\) along \(y\), so \(b/a = \sqrt{1 - e^2}\), and the pressure is \(p(x, y) = \dfrac{3F}{2A}\sqrt{1 - x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2}\) (a semi-ellipsoid).

Source: BOWER, §5.4.11 (PDF pp. 333-334): the equations for \(R_1\), \(R_2\), \(e\), \(A\) (crops p333-b1, p334-b1, p334-b3, p334-b4). HK, §6.3 (PDF pp. 127-129): the same with the parameter \(\kappa\) and Table 6.1. Cited, not proved. If \(R_2/R_1 \to 1\), \(e \to 0\) and the solution passes into theorem 25.27 (checked: \(R_2/R_1 = 1{,}01\) gives an area \(1{,}0033\) times \(\pi a^2\) of the sphere, num-06.py E).

We test this with the groove. We solve equation (25.26) with \(R_2/R_1 = 32{,}60\) numerically (bisection, mpmath) and get \(e = 0{,}99425\) and \(b/a = 0{,}1071\). For \(F = 100\) N, \(A = 0{,}1786\) mm\(^2\), \(a = 728\ \mu\text{m}\), \(b = 78{,}0\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(p_0 = 3F/(2A) = 840\) MPa. For \(1000\) N, \(A = 0{,}8288\) mm\(^2\), \(a = 1569\ \mu\text{m}\), \(b = 168{,}1\ \mu\text{m}\), \(p_0 = 1810\) MPa, while the pressure of the same ball on a plane is \(3818\) MPa. A fitting groove therefore reduces the pressure to about \(47\ \%\), which is the reason bearings do not have flat raceways. We also check HK Table 6.1 (PDF p. 129): at \(\Phi = 0{,}9405\) linear interpolation in it gives \(k = a/b \approx 9{,}4\), our value is \(1/0{,}1071 = 9{,}34\), which agrees to \(1\ \%\) (the interpolation is approximate).

When the surfaces fit too well. The Hertz calculation required the gap \(x^2/(2R_2) + y^2/(2R_1)\) to be accurate enough. With a fitting raceway this is not as good. In the transverse plane the gap is the difference of two almost equal arcs and the error of the parabola does not stay small: at \(F = 1000\) N, at the edge of the contact, \(a = 1{,}569\) mm, the true gap is \(7{,}801\ \mu\text{m}\) against the parabola's \(7{,}455\ \mu\text{m}\), which is a \(4{,}6\ \%\) error (at \(100\) N \(1{,}0\ \%\)), while for a sphere on a plane we had \(0{,}078\ \%\). So the results of theorem 25.31 for more fitting contacts (osculation toward \(1\)) are no longer reliable and must be checked with more exact geometry, which we do not derive here. The third property of a nonconformal contact (definition 25.18), that the contact is small and that the surfaces near it follow the curvatures well, is therefore only approximately satisfied in a fitting raceway.

This section gave all three quantities for the contact of a sphere: radius, approach and pressure, and for the groove the ellipse. The next section places these contacts in a bearing: \(K h^{3/2}\) from theorem 25.27 becomes the force-displacement law of one ball (section 25.7).

Notation of this section. The letter \(E^*\) is an italic scalar, the bold \(\mat E^*\) is the Euler-Almansi strain. The letter \(R\) is the radius of a sphere and the effective radius, not the radius of curvature of the wall of the beam from section 25.4, where \(R\) is the distance from the point of the force. The letter \(h\) is the approach after BOWER, in the following sections \(\delta\). The letter \(a\) is the radius of the contact circle or a semi-axis of the ellipse and is not the radius of the tube of chapter 11. The letter \(\Phi\) is the curvature difference (HK: \(F(\rho)\)). The letter \(F\) is the force, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) is the yield stress (definition 2.7).

25.7 Load on a rolling bearing

A shaft supported by a bearing presses on it with a force. In a bearing with nine steel balls of diameter \(D = 12{,}7\) mm let the shaft press with a force \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 1000\) N perpendicular to the axis. Does every ball carry a ninth of this force, that is \(111{,}1\) N? The balls on the upper side of the shaft cannot carry it: a ball can only support the shaft, it cannot pull it down. So only some balls will carry force, most of all the one under the shaft. How much exactly the most loaded ball carries decides which contact we must compute by section 25.6 and how stiffly the bearing supports the shaft (section 25.8). This section therefore first builds a model of the bearing, then derives from the contact of two bodies the law between the force of a ball and its displacement, and at the end computes the distribution of the force among the balls from the equilibrium of the ring.

Let us draw the bearing as we see it when cut perpendicular to the axis. First the outer ring. It is fixed in the housing and stands still. Its inner side is the raceway (steza), because the balls run along it like runners on a track. Between the rings are nine balls. They roll on the raceways, so friction is small, and this is why the bearing is called rolling (kotalni, from kotaliti, to roll). The balls must not collide. So a cage (kletka) holds them, placing them at equal angular spacings and leaving them free to roll. It is named for the way it closes the balls in like bars. We do not draw the cage in the figure, since it only keeps the spacings. From the middle the balls are touched by the inner ring, on which the shaft is mounted. The bearing (ležaj) is named for the shaft lying (ležati) on it and resting against it.

The shaft acts on it with the force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\), which we draw from the centre of the inner ring downward, because the shaft pushes the ring there. A force (sila) is what changes the motion of a body or deforms it, measured in newtons. The load (obremenitev) is the force with which the bearing is loaded from outside, named for the burden (breme). The index \(r\) says that the force is radial (radialna), that is perpendicular to the axis. Under this force the rings are in equilibrium (ravnovesje), that is, the sum of all forces on them is zero and they do not accelerate. We will use the equilibrium below.

Under the force the inner ring shifts downward by a distance \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) toward the outer one, drawn with edge marks between the centres of the two rings. The ball under the axis is squeezed between the rings, and the ball at the top gets room. For each ball we need the angle \(\psi\) that its axis measures from the vertical along which the force acts. The balls in the load zone are squeezed, in the figure from \(-\psi_{\mathrm{l}}\) to \(\psi_{\mathrm{l}}\).

Definition 25.32 Radial rolling-element bearing (radialni kotalni ležaj)

A radial ball bearing has an inner and an outer ring, between them \(Z\) equal balls of diameter \(D\) and a cage that places the balls at equal angular spacings \(2\pi/Z\). The rings have raceways along which the balls roll. In an unloaded bearing in which the axes of both rings coincide, the diametral clearance (diametralna zračnost) \(P_{\mathrm{d}} \ge 0\) is the difference between the diameter of the outer raceway and the sum of the diameter of the inner raceway and two ball diameters. The angle \(\alpha\) between the radial plane and the line along which the ball pushes on the rings is the contact angle (stični kot). For a radial bearing \(\alpha = 0\). The force \(Q\) with which a ring presses on a ball at the point of contact and perpendicular to the surface is the rolling-element load (obremenitev kroglice). The force with which the shaft loads the bearing perpendicular to the axis is the radial load \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the force along the axis is the axial load (osna obremenitev) \(F_{\mathrm{a}}\).

Source: The notions follow FPGL section 5.5.3 (PDF p. 201-202), which lists the rings, raceways, balls and cage, and HK section 7.1 (PDF p. 155). The clearance and the contact angle follow HK (PDF p. 156 and 160). The claims are not proved, the definition only fixes the names.

The model we use has a number of simplifications, which we name so that they do not drop out of sight.

  • The rings are rigid: they do not deform, they move as a whole. Real rings bend. This neglects the compliance of the housing and the ring, which is visible in light housings.
  • There is no friction and no inertia of the balls: the forces in the contact are perpendicular to the surface, the balls are in equilibrium. HK (PDF p. 155) justifies this by noting that rotation speeds are usually not so high that the inertial forces of the balls would affect the distribution. In a fast bearing the centrifugal force would change the load on the outer raceway, which chapter 24 treats.
  • The contact of a ball and a raceway is a non-conforming contact by definition 25.18, its stresses and stiffness are described by the Hertz solution of section 25.6. Lubrication and friction in the contact, which are outside this chapter, do not appear in the model.
  • The load is static: the shaft is at rest or turns slowly enough that we can compute the equilibrium.

A ball in the bearing has two contacts, with the inner and with the outer raceway. Before we compute what force it carries, we must know which force corresponds to which displacement. This is the force-approach law for one contact.

Let us draw a ball of radius \(D/2\) and squeeze it between two walls. The lower inner raceway approaches the ball by \(\delta_{\mathrm{i}}\), the outer one by \(\delta_{\mathrm{o}}\). Both displacements are measured from the place where the walls touched, so the total approach of the two raceways is the sum \(\delta = \delta_{\mathrm{i}} + \delta_{\mathrm{o}}\). The ball is in equilibrium under two forces. There is no friction, so each of the two forces is perpendicular to the surface of the sphere and passes through its centre. In equilibrium the sum of the forces is zero, so the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. Since both pass through the centre, they lie on the same line through both points of contact. This is the same force \(Q\) in both contacts.

What is the law of a single contact? For a spring we know \(F = kx\). For a Hertz contact the force is not proportional to the approach, since at a larger force the contact area is also larger and so the contact is stiffer. This holds for every contact whose gap before loading is a quadratic function:

Lemma 25.33 Force-approach law of a contact (zakon sila-pomik stika)

Let two bodies touch in a non-conforming contact (definition 25.18) under the Hertz assumptions, and let them be linearly elastic and isotropic with effective modulus \(E^*\). Let the gap before loading in the principal axes of the contact be \(g_0(x, y) = Ax^2 + By^2\) with \(A, B > 0\) (definition 25.30), and let the approach (približevanje) of the bodies, which we wrote \(h\) in theorem 25.27, be written \(\delta\) in this section.

  1. If the contact problem (the conditions of definition 25.19, written in the plane of contact with given \(\delta\) at the start of the proof) has exactly one solution at every \(\delta > 0\), the force in the contact is
    \[Q = K\,\delta^{3/2} \tag{25.28}\]
    with a number \(K > 0\) independent of \(\delta\).
  2. A ball touching two raceways with the numbers \(K_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(K_{\mathrm{o}}\) from item 1 carries the same force \(Q\) at both contacts, their total approach is \(\delta = \delta_{\mathrm{i}} + \delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) and \(Q = K_{\mathrm{n}}\,\delta^{3/2}\) holds with
    \[K_{\mathrm{n}} = \Big( K_{\mathrm{i}}^{-2/3} + K_{\mathrm{o}}^{-2/3} \Big)^{-3/2} . \tag{25.29}\]
Idea

If we double the approach, the contact area widens and the pressure rises. We show that a stretching of space in the ratio \(\sqrt\lambda\) maps the solution for \(\delta\) to a solution for \(\lambda\delta\), which determines how the force changes. The second item we get from the equilibrium of the ball.

Proof

Denote by \(\Omega\) the contact region, which is to be closed and convex, and by \(p \ge 0\) a continuous pressure, which is zero outside \(\Omega\). By lemma 25.17 and theorem 25.15, added for both bodies with the effective modulus of definition 25.21, the total displacement of both surfaces toward the interior in the model, measured from far away, at the point \(\vek x\) of the surface is

\[u(\vek x) = \frac{1}{\pi E^*} \int_\Omega \frac{p(\vek s)}{|\vek x - \vek s|}\,\mathrm{d}A_{\vek{s}} .\]

The contact problem at a given \(\delta > 0\) consists of the conditions of definition 25.19 written in the plane of contact: the gap is zero on \(\Omega\), \(g_0(\vek x) + u(\vek x) - \delta = 0\), outside \(\Omega\) we have \(g_0 + u - \delta \ge 0\), and the pressure is non-negative. The approach \(\delta\) is given, and the force \(Q = \int_\Omega p\,\mathrm{d}A\) is unknown.

  1. Let the triple \((\Omega, p, \delta)\) solve the contact problem. For \(\lambda > 0\) define \(\Omega_\lambda = \sqrt\lambda\,\Omega\), \(p_\lambda(\vek x) = \sqrt\lambda\,p(\vek x/\sqrt\lambda)\) and \(\delta_\lambda = \lambda\delta\). We must show that the triple \((\Omega_\lambda, p_\lambda, \delta_\lambda)\) solves the same problem.
  2. Substitute \(\vek s = \sqrt\lambda\,\vek s'\) and \(\vek x = \sqrt\lambda\,\vek x'\). Then \(|\vek x - \vek s| = \sqrt\lambda\,|\vek x' - \vek s'|\) and \(p_\lambda(\vek s) = \sqrt\lambda\,p(\vek s')\). The map \(\vek s' \mapsto \sqrt\lambda\,\vek s'\) stretches the plane by \(\sqrt\lambda\) in each of two directions, its Jacobian determinant is \(\lambda\), and by theorem 4.59 the integral gets the factor \(\lambda\). Hence
    \[u_\lambda(\vek x) = \frac{1}{\pi E^*} \int_{\Omega} \frac{\sqrt\lambda\,p(\vek s')}{\sqrt\lambda\,|\vek x' - \vek s'|}\,\lambda\,\mathrm{d}A_{\vek{s}'} = \lambda\,u(\vek x') .\]
  3. The function \(g_0\) is homogeneous quadratic: \(g_0(\vek x) = \lambda\,g_0(\vek x')\). Hence \(g_0(\vek x) + u_\lambda(\vek x) - \delta_\lambda = \lambda\big(g_0(\vek x') + u(\vek x') - \delta\big)\). This is zero on \(\Omega_\lambda\) and non-negative outside it, since \(\vek x' \in \Omega\) exactly when \(\vek x \in \Omega_\lambda\). The pressure \(p_\lambda\) is non-negative and continuous, and \(\Omega_\lambda\) is closed and convex. So \((\Omega_\lambda, p_\lambda, \delta_\lambda)\) is a solution (definition 25.19).
  4. The force is the integral of the pressure over \(\Omega_\lambda\): \(Q_\lambda = \int_{\Omega_\lambda} p_\lambda\,\mathrm{d}A = \sqrt\lambda \cdot \lambda \int_\Omega p\,\mathrm{d}A = \lambda^{3/2}\,Q\). The factor \(\lambda\) is the Jacobian determinant of step 2 (theorem 4.59), and \(\sqrt\lambda\) is the factor of the pressure.
  5. Since the solution at each approach is unique (the assumption of item 1), \(Q(\lambda\delta) = \lambda^{3/2}\,Q(\delta)\) for all \(\lambda > 0\) and \(\delta > 0\). With \(\lambda = \delta/\delta_1\) at a chosen \(\delta_1 > 0\) we get \(Q(\delta) = Q(\delta_1)\,\delta_1^{-3/2}\,\delta^{3/2}\), and \(K = Q(\delta_1)\,\delta_1^{-3/2}\) does not depend on \(\delta\). At the point \(\vek x = 0\) we have \(g_0(0) = 0\), so the gap condition gives \(u(0) \ge \delta_1 > 0\). The pressure is therefore not zero everywhere, and since it is continuous and non-negative, \(Q(\delta_1) = \int_\Omega p\,\mathrm{d}A > 0\), so \(K > 0\). This is item 1.
  6. We cut the ball out of the bearing and draw all forces on it. It touches only two bodies and there is no friction, so only two forces act on it (figure 25.26). Equilibrium requires that their sum is zero, so they are equal in size and opposite in direction. The same force \(Q\) therefore acts at both contacts.
  7. We measure both approaches to the centre of the ball, which we take as far from both contacts (at \(1000\) N the contact radius is \(5{,}6\,\%\) of the ball radius, see below), so the deformation at one contact does not move the other and the approaches add. By item 1, \(Q = K_{\mathrm{i}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{i}}^{3/2} = K_{\mathrm{o}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{o}}^{3/2}\), so \(\delta_{\mathrm{i}} = (Q/K_{\mathrm{i}})^{2/3}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{o}} = (Q/K_{\mathrm{o}})^{2/3}\). The sum is \(\delta = Q^{2/3}\big(K_{\mathrm{i}}^{-2/3} + K_{\mathrm{o}}^{-2/3}\big)\). Inverting gives \(Q = \delta^{3/2}\big(K_{\mathrm{i}}^{-2/3} + K_{\mathrm{o}}^{-2/3}\big)^{-3/2}\). This is item 2.

Source: Item 2 follows HK (7.5) to (7.7) (PDF p. 156), which writes the series of two contacts with \(\delta_{\mathrm{n}} = \delta_{\mathrm{i}} + \delta_{\mathrm{o}}\). The exponent \(3/2\) in item 1 follows HK (7.2) (PDF p. 155) and BOWER (PDF p. 331), where it is obtained from the Hertz solution. The proof by scaling is not from the source. The book does not prove the uniqueness of the contact problem (theorem 11.4 holds for bounded bodies and regular data, not for contact).

Let us test the law on a ball \(D = 12{,}7\) mm between two flat steel plates of the book (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\), so \(E^* = E/(2(1-\nu^2)) = 107\,692\) MPa and \(R = 6{,}35\) mm). By theorem 25.27 \(F = \tfrac43 E^*\sqrt R\,h^{3/2}\), so \(K = \tfrac43 E^*\sqrt R = 361\,835\) N/mm\(^{3/2}\). At \(Q = 1000\) N, \(\delta_{\mathrm{i}} = \delta_{\mathrm{o}} = 19{,}69\) µm, together \(\delta = 39{,}39\) µm, and \(K_{\mathrm{n}} = 1000/\delta^{3/2} = 127\,928\) N/mm\(^{3/2}\). By equation (25.29), \(K_{\mathrm{n}} = \big(2K^{-2/3}\big)^{-3/2} = K/2^{3/2} = 127\,928\) N/mm\(^{3/2}\), the same number, since \(2^{-3/2} = 0{,}3536\). Two contacts in series are thus softer than one. Let us also check the scaling: at \(\lambda = 2\), \(Q(2h)/Q(h) = 2{,}828 = 2^{3/2}\), and at \(\lambda = 10\), \(31{,}62 = 10^{3/2}\).

Is it sensible to use the lemma for our balls? It requires the Hertz assumptions, among them that the contact area is small. At \(Q = 1000\) N the radius of the contact circle is \(a = 353{,}6\) µm (section 25.6, the example with a ball), which is \(5{,}6\,\%\) of the ball radius \(6{,}35\) mm, so the quadratic form of the gap \(Ax^2 + By^2\) near the contact is accurate. The lemma does not hold for cylinders: in a line contact the area of the contact line is not small relative to the size of the bodies, and the displacement of the plane in the Flamant solution (section 25.3) contains terms \(\ln r\) that depend on the size of the bodies. For a line contact the law with the power \(3/2\) therefore cannot be derived. For roller bearings HK gives (7.3) \(Q = K_{\mathrm{l}}\,\delta^{10/9}\) (PDF p. 155 and 156) as a law from measurements and computations, which the book does not prove (lemma 25.25). It also fails for a contact where the surfaces fit closely (a conforming contact, which definition 25.18 excludes), since the contact area is no longer small relative to the radii of curvature and the half-space is not a good model. In both cases the law \(Q = K\delta^n\) will have another exponent \(n\) or another constant. For ball bearings \(n = 3/2\), for roller bearings \(n = 10/9\) (HK (7.4), PDF p. 156), in what follows we write in general \(Q = K_{\mathrm{n}}\,\delta^n\), and the proofs shown hold for every \(n \ge 1\).

Now we compute how the force is distributed. Let us write down what the shift of the ring means for an individual ball, and introduce the variables.

Definition 25.34 Radial shift of the ring and the load zone (radialni pomik obroča in območje obremenitve)

For a bearing of definition 25.32 let the outer ring be fixed and let the inner ring shift as a whole by a number \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) in the direction of the force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\). The balls are at the angles \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}} = \psi_0 + 2\pi j/Z\) \((j = 0, \dots, Z - 1)\), measured from the direction of the force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) (figure 25.25), where \(\psi_0\) gives the position of the cage. For \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} > P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\) we define the load-zone parameter (parameter obremenitvenega območja)

\[\chi = \frac12\Big(1 - \frac{P_{\mathrm{d}}}{2\delta_{\mathrm{r}}}\Big) \tag{25.30}\]

and the limit angle \(\psi_{\mathrm{l}} = \arccos\big(P_{\mathrm{d}}/(2\delta_{\mathrm{r}})\big) = \arccos(1 - 2\chi)\). The balls at the angles \(|\psi_{\mathrm{j}}| < \psi_{\mathrm{l}}\) are in the load zone (območje obremenitve).

Source: By HK (7.10) to (7.13) (PDF p. 156-157). HK writes the parameter \(\varepsilon\), the book uses the letter \(\varepsilon\) for strain, so we write \(\chi\). The sum introduced in the next theorem follows HK (7.16) and (7.17) (PDF p. 158).

In an unloaded bearing with clearance \(P_{\mathrm{d}}\) and concentric rings, at the place of each ball the sum of the gaps between the ball and the two raceways is \(P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\) (the clearance \(P_{\mathrm{d}}\) divides over two balls at opposite ends of a diameter). The inner ring shifts under the force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the gap under it closes. The ball under the axis truly touches when \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} > P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\). So \(\chi > 0\) exactly when the bearing is really loaded, and \(\chi \le 1/2\) because \(P_{\mathrm{d}} \ge 0\). At zero clearance \(\chi = 1/2\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{l}} = 90^\circ\): the whole lower half is loaded.

For each ball we must know two things: how the distance between the raceways changes when the ring shifts, and what force this causes. The first is given by geometry, the second by lemma 25.33. Then we write the equilibrium of the inner ring.

We draw the inner ring alone, as a ring, and replace everything that acts on it by forces. The shaft pushes it with the downward force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\). The ring is carried by the balls, which push it toward the centre at the points of contact. We draw each of these forces of the balls on its own radial line and each arrow ends at the point of contact with the ring, because the force is a push. The ball under the shaft carries the most, the neighbours each less, so the arrows are shorter. Since all the forces of the balls pass through the centre of the ring, they give no moment. For the equilibrium of the ring what remains is that the sum of forces along \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) is zero: the forces of the balls, projected on this direction, carry \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Theorem 25.35 Distribution of a radial load among the balls (porazdelitev radialne obremenitve med kroglice)

Let there be a bearing of definition 25.32 with rigid rings, without friction and inertial forces, with \(Z \ge 3\) balls and clearance \(P_{\mathrm{d}} \ge 0\), at radial load \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) and radial shift \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} > P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\) (definition 25.34). Let a ball in contact with both raceways follow the law \(Q = K_{\mathrm{n}}\,\delta^n\) with the same \(n \ge 1\) and \(K_{\mathrm{n}}\) for all balls (for balls from lemma 25.33 with \(n = 3/2\), for rollers HK (7.4) with \(n = 10/9\)). Let \(Q_{\max} = K_{\mathrm{n}}(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} - P_{\mathrm{d}}/2)^n\).

  1. The approach of the raceways at the ball at the angle \(\psi\) is \(\delta_\psi = \delta_{\mathrm{r}}\cos\psi - P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\), up to a term of second order in \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\), which is at most \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}^2/(2R_{\mathrm{p}})\), where \(R_{\mathrm{p}}\) is the radius of the circle of ball centres, and the ball is loaded exactly when \(\delta_\psi > 0\), that is \(|\psi| < \psi_{\mathrm{l}}\).
  2. The load of the ball at the angle \(\psi\) in the load zone is
    \[Q_\psi = Q_{\max}\Big[1 - \frac{1 - \cos\psi}{2\chi}\Big]^n , \tag{25.31}\]
    and outside it is zero.
  3. If the cage is such that the direction of the force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) lies in a symmetry line of the bearing (one ball on the direction of the force or between two balls), then
    \[F_{\mathrm{r}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} Q_{\psi_\mathrm{j}}\cos\psi_{\mathrm{j}} . \tag{25.32}\]
  4. Let
    \[J_{\mathrm{r}}(\chi) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\psi_\mathrm{l}}^{\psi_{\mathrm{l}}} \Big[1 - \frac{1 - \cos\psi}{2\chi}\Big]^n\cos\psi\;\mathrm{d}\psi . \tag{25.33}\]
    Then \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = Z\,Q_{\max}\,J_{\mathrm{r}}(\chi) + \eta\) with \(|\eta| \le 2\,Q_{\max}\). In other words, \(\big|F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z\,Q_{\max}) - J_{\mathrm{r}}(\chi)\big| \le 2/Z\).
Idea

The shift of the ring determines the approach of each ball by geometry, the contact law gives the force, and the equilibrium of the ring gives the sum. We replace the sum over the balls by an integral over the angle, which is a Riemann sum, and estimate it.

Proof
  1. When the ring shifts by \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) in the direction \(\psi = 0\), the distance between the centres of the raceways at the ball at the angle \(\psi\) changes by the projection of the shift on the radial line, \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\cos\psi\), with an error of second order in \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\), which is at most \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}^2/(2R_{\mathrm{p}})\). At \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = 11{,}54\) µm (the shift of the bearing of the introduction at \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 1000\) N, computed in section 25.8) and a radius of the circle of ball centres \(R_{\mathrm{p}} = 23\) mm (assumed, a bearing for balls \(D = 12{,}7\) mm) this term is \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}^2/(2R_{\mathrm{p}}) = 2{,}9\) nm, \(0{,}025\,\%\) of the shift, so we neglect it. The sum of the gaps between the ball and the two raceways before loading is \(P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\) (by definition 25.32 the diameter \(P_{\mathrm{d}}\) divides over two balls at opposite ends of a diameter), which is subtracted, and \(\delta_\psi = \delta_{\mathrm{r}}\cos\psi - P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\). If \(\delta_\psi \le 0\), the ball does not touch both raceways. The contact does not pull (definition 25.19, pressure \(\ge 0\)), so \(Q = 0\). It is therefore loaded exactly for \(\cos\psi > P_{\mathrm{d}}/(2\delta_{\mathrm{r}})\), that is \(|\psi| < \psi_{\mathrm{l}}\).
  2. By the assumed contact law, \(Q_\psi = K_{\mathrm{n}}\,\delta_\psi^n\). At \(\psi = 0\), \(\delta_0 = \delta_{\mathrm{r}} - P_{\mathrm{d}}/2 = 2\chi\,\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) (equation (25.30)), so \(Q_{\max} = K_{\mathrm{n}}\,\delta_0^n\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = \delta_0/(2\chi)\). Hence \(\delta_\psi = \delta_0 + \delta_{\mathrm{r}}(\cos\psi - 1) = \delta_0\big[1 - (1 - \cos\psi)/(2\chi)\big]\), and substituting into \(Q_\psi = K_{\mathrm{n}}\delta_\psi^n\) gives equation (25.31).
  3. The inner ring is in equilibrium under the force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the forces of the balls (figure 25.27). The force of ball \(j\) on the ring is \(Q_{\psi_\mathrm{j}}\) along the radial line at the angle \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\), directed toward the centre. Its component against the direction in which \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) acts is \(Q_{\psi_\mathrm{j}}\cos\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\). The perpendicular component of the force of a pair of balls at \(\pm\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) cancels by symmetry about the direction of \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\), because the loads are equal, and what remains is the sum along \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\), which must balance \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\). This is equation (25.32). The forces pass through the centre of the ring, so there is no moment.
  4. Define \(f(\psi) = [1 - (1 - \cos\psi)/(2\chi)]^n\cos\psi\) on \([-\psi_{\mathrm{l}}, \psi_{\mathrm{l}}]\) and \(f(\psi) = 0\) elsewhere on \([-\pi, \pi)\), then extend it with period \(2\pi\). For \(\chi \le 1/2\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{l}} \le \pi/2\), and \(f\) is non-negative, continuous (\(f(\pm\psi_{\mathrm{l}}) = 0\)), even, and decreasing on \([0, \pi]\) (a product of two non-negative decreasing functions, \(\cos\psi\) and the bracket, which both decrease for \(\psi\) between \(0\) and \(\psi_{\mathrm{l}}\), after which \(f = 0\)), \(f(0) = 1\). By theorem 3.38, \(J_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f\,\mathrm{d}\psi\) is well defined. The integral of a periodic function is the same over every interval of length \(2\pi\), so also \(J_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\psi_0}^{\psi_0 + 2\pi} f\,\mathrm{d}\psi\), and this interval is covered by the cells of step 5.
  5. By equation (25.32) and step 2, \(F_{\mathrm{r}}/Q_{\max} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} f(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})\), since \(f(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})\) is the value \([\dots]^n\cos\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) for the balls in the zone and zero for the others. The angular spacing is \(\Delta = 2\pi/Z\). So \(F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z\,Q_{\max}) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} f(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta\) (a Riemann sum with the left edges of the cells). We compare it with the integral over the cells \([\psi_{\mathrm{j}}, \psi_{\mathrm{j}} + \Delta]\).
  6. On each cell \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(|f(\psi) - f(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})| \le v_{\mathrm{j}}\), where \(v_{\mathrm{j}} = \max_{\mathrm{c}_\mathrm{j}} f - \min_{\mathrm{c}_\mathrm{j}} f\) is the oscillation of \(f\) on the cell (a continuous \(f\) has a largest and a smallest value on a closed cell). Hence \(\big|\int_{\mathrm{c}_\mathrm{j}} f\,\mathrm{d}\psi - f(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta\big| \le v_{\mathrm{j}}\,\Delta\) (lemma 3.35 gives a bound for the integral, the estimate is direct from \(|f - f(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})| \le v_{\mathrm{j}}\)). In one period \(f\) rises from \(0\) to \(1\) and falls back to \(0\). On a cell where \(f\) is monotone, \(v_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the change of \(f\) on it, and these changes add up to at most \(1\) on the rising part and at most \(1\) on the falling part. The cell with the peak contributes at most the rise to the left of the peak plus the fall to its right. So \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} v_{\mathrm{j}} \le 2\).
  7. Adding up: \(\big|\sum_{\mathrm{j}} f(\psi_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta - \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f\,\mathrm{d}\psi\big| \le 2\Delta\). Dividing by \(2\pi\): \(\big|F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z\,Q_{\max}) - J_{\mathrm{r}}\big| \le 2\Delta/(2\pi) = 2/Z\).

Source: The geometry and equations (25.31) to (25.33) follow HK (7.10) to (7.20) (PDF p. 156-158). HK calls the integral \(J_{\mathrm{r}}\) the radial integral and tabulates it (table 7.1, PDF p. 158). The estimate \(2/Z\) of the error of the sum is not from the source. The neglect of the side force at cage positions that are not symmetric is described in the text.

What has the theorem shown? For a given load we know how \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) is distributed if we know a single parameter, \(\chi\). The load falls from the ball under the shaft toward the edge of the zone, as the blue curve in figure 25.28 shows, where for zero clearance (\(\chi = 1/2\), \(n = 3/2\)) \(Q_\psi/Q_{\max} = \cos^{3/2}\psi\) for \(|\psi| < 90^\circ\). The equilibrium gives what we are looking for: from \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\chi\) the largest force \(Q_{\max}\), and from it the shift \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Let us draw an axis, the angle \(\psi\) from \(-90^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\) on the horizontal and the load in units of \(Q_{\max}\) on the vertical. The load of a ball that would be on the direction of the force, in the continuous curve, falls as \(\cos^{3/2}\psi\). The balls, which really are at separate angles, we draw as bars: with nine balls the angular spacings are \(40^\circ\), and when one ball is on the direction of the force, the bars are at \(0^\circ\), \(\pm 40^\circ\) and \(\pm 80^\circ\) with heights \(1\), \(0{,}6705\) and \(0{,}0724\) (\(Q_{\max}\) times \(\cos^{3/2}\) at these angles). When the cage turns by \(20^\circ\), the balls are at other angles, \(\pm 20^\circ\) and \(\pm 60^\circ\), with heights \(0{,}9109\) and \(0{,}3536\). The tallest bar at the second cage position is \(9\,\%\) lower than the largest value of the curve, because no ball is at the place of the maximum.

If we neglect the error \(\eta\) of item 4 of the theorem, we get the integral model, which we use for the computation:

\[F_{\mathrm{r}} \approx Z\,Q_{\max}\,J_{\mathrm{r}}(\chi) , \qquad Q_{\max} = K_{\mathrm{n}}(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} - P_{\mathrm{d}}/2)^n . \tag{25.34}\]

For a given \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) the unknown is \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) (and with it \(\chi\)), since \(J_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a tabulated function of \(\chi\). HK solves the equation by trial: he chooses \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\), computes \(\chi\) by equation (25.30), reads off \(J_{\mathrm{r}}\) and checks the equation (PDF p. 159).

Example 25.36 A bearing with nine balls (ležaj z devetimi kroglicami)

For the bearing of the introduction, \(Z = 9\), \(D = 12{,}7\) mm, zero clearance (\(\chi = 1/2\), \(\psi_{\mathrm{l}} = 90^\circ\)) and \(n = 3/2\), \(J_{\mathrm{r}}(1/2) = 0{,}2288\) (numerical quadrature of equation (25.33), equal to HK table 7.1, PDF p. 158). By the integral model (25.34), \(Q_{\max} = F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z\,J_{\mathrm{r}}) = 1000/(9 \cdot 0{,}2288) = 485{,}6\) N, not \(111{,}1\) N. When a ball is on the direction of the force, by equation (25.31) the forces at \(0^\circ\), \(\pm 40^\circ\), \(\pm 80^\circ\) are \(485{,}6\) N, \(325{,}6\) N and \(35{,}1\) N, and the other four balls do not carry. Check of the equilibrium by equation (25.32): \(485{,}6 + 2 \cdot 325{,}6\cos 40^\circ + 2 \cdot 35{,}1\cos 80^\circ = 996{,}7\) N. Up to \(1000\) N, \(0{,}34\,\%\) is missing, which is the error of the integral model, bounded by \(2/Z\) in item 4 of the theorem.

The integral is not always a good substitute for the sum. The first reason is the position of the cage, the second the small number of balls in the load zone. Let us look at both.

First, the integral replaces a sum. With \(Z = 9\) balls the angular spacing is \(40^\circ\), and whether a ball is on the direction of the force affects the result. The largest load that any of the balls carries at a given force \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) is, at the two positions of the cage (for a ball on the direction of the force this is \(Q_{\max}\) of the theorem, for the position between two balls it is less, since there is no ball at the angle \(0^\circ\)):

\(Z\) ball on the direction of the force between two balls bound \(2/Z\) for \(F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z Q_{\max})\)
8 \(4{,}346\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(3{,}899\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(0{,}250\)
9 \(4{,}385\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(3{,}969\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(0{,}222\)
12 \(4{,}364\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(4{,}153\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(0{,}167\)
16 \(4{,}368\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(4{,}246\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(0{,}125\)
36 \(4{,}370\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(4{,}345\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(0{,}056\)
100 \(4{,}370\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(4{,}367\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) \(0{,}020\)

The integral with its value \(4{,}370\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\) is close to the larger of the two values (a ball on the direction of the force): at \(Z = 9\) it is \(0{,}3\,\%\) below it, at \(Z = 8\) \(0{,}6\,\%\) above it. The bound \(2/Z\) of the theorem is coarse: at \(Z = 9\) it is \(0{,}222\), almost as much as the value \(J_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}2288\) itself (\(97\,\%\)), so the proof alone does not yet say that the integral is good for such sparse balls. It only says that the error is not larger than \(2/Z\). The actual error falls much faster: with a ball on the direction of the force, \(F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z\,Q_{\max})\) differs from \(J_{\mathrm{r}}\) by \(0{,}56\,\%\) at \(Z = 8\), by \(0{,}13\,\%\) at \(Z = 12\) and by \(0{,}05\,\%\) at \(Z = 16\), so more than ten times less from \(Z = 8\) to \(Z = 16\). The actual deviation of \(F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z\,Q_{\max})\) from \(J_{\mathrm{r}}\) at the same shift of the ring is at \(Z = 9\) only \(-0{,}34\,\%\) and \(+0{,}29\,\%\), since the errors of the cage position average out in the sum, but the deviation of the largest load at a given force reaches \(9\,\%\) (\(11\,\%\) at \(Z = 8\)), since a ball is not necessarily at the place of the largest load. At intermediate positions of the cage, for example \(10^\circ\) at \(Z = 9\), the result is no longer symmetric, and the side component of the sum of forces on the ring reaches \(1{,}3\,\%\) of \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\). The ring would really also move sideways, which we neglect, because the theorem holds for the symmetric positions (item 3). The two symmetric positions bound the largest ball load: \(4{,}385\) at \(0^\circ\), \(4{,}355\) at \(5^\circ\), \(4{,}270\) at \(10^\circ\), \(4{,}139\) at \(15^\circ\) and \(3{,}969\) at \(20^\circ\) in units of \(F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\).

Second, at large clearance and light load the load zone is narrow. Let \(P_{\mathrm{d}} = 20\) µm and \(\chi = 0{,}1\). Then \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = P_{\mathrm{d}}/(2(1 - 2\chi)) = 12{,}50\) µm, \(\delta_0 = 2{,}50\) µm and \(\psi_{\mathrm{l}} = \arccos 0{,}8 = 36{,}87^\circ\). The integral gives \(J_{\mathrm{r}}(0{,}1) = 0{,}1156\) and \(Q_{\max} = 8{,}653\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\). With \(Z = 9\) balls at a spacing of \(40^\circ\), the zone \(\pm 36{,}87^\circ\) can hold only one ball (if it is on the direction of the force) or two, at \(\pm 20^\circ\). In the first case \(Q_{\max} = F_{\mathrm{r}} = 9{,}000\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\), in the second \(4{,}789\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\). Here the integral is not a good model of the sum, because there are so few balls in the zone that the Riemann sum has one or two points. With the approximation \(Q_{\max} = 5\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/(Z\cos\alpha)\) for clearance (equation (7.24), PDF p. 159), HK expressly warns that it does not suffice for light loads. Third, the theorem assumes rigid rings. With elastic rings the zone would widen, because the ring would give way under the largest ball and pass its burden to the neighbours. The model does not capture this (section 25.9 shows where the elasticity of the rings does not appear in the model).

Corollary 25.37 Maximum ball load at zero clearance (največja obremenitev kroglice pri ničelni zračnosti)

For a bearing with rigid rings, zero clearance (\(\chi = 1/2\)), \(Z\) balls and radial load \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\), in the model of theorem 25.35 with \(n = 3/2\)
