It is a straight line through the origin, so the force changes sign with the displacement and the foundation also pulls. The penalty term \(\tfrac12\,\alpha\,|\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g|^2\) of definition 12.27 has the same form, since the force \(-\alpha\,(\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g)\) is two-sided. The Winkler foundation is therefore a penalty on the constraint \(v = 0\) along the whole length of the beam, a penalty that we choose as we choose \(\alpha\). In contact the bodies must not pull on each other, so the middle law is zero for \(\delta < 0\) and for \(\delta > 0\) a linear spring with \(\alpha\). With this the pressure of definition 25.19 is always non-negative, and the product of pressure and gap is zero only in the limit \(\alpha \to \infty\), while for finite \(\alpha\) the bodies penetrate by \(F/\alpha\). Theorem 12.28 proves this for equality constraints, for one-sided ones the book does not prove it. The right law is the Hertz law: the force is zero as long as the bodies do not touch, then grows as \(\delta^{3/2}\) by theorem 25.27 and corollary 25.28. Penetration here is not an error of the method. It is the approach by which the bodies really come closer, because they are compressed around the contact, and \(K = \tfrac43\,E^*\sqrt R\) is given by the material and the radius (\(E^*\) and \(R\) from section 25.6), not chosen. A penalty number chosen for one load does not hold for another: the tangent stiffness of a steel ball of diameter \(12{,}7\) mm on a steel flat body is \(35\,353\) N/mm at \(100\) N and \(76\,167\) N/mm at \(1000\) N (section 25.6), so more than twice as large.

What are the secant and the tangent for the Hertz law? The static approach is computed from the secant, \(\delta = F/k_{\mathrm{s}}\), and a small vibration about the state is described by the tangent \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\) (theorem 25.51, which uses theorem 8.60). For the power \(F = K\,\delta^{3/2}\) we have \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = \tfrac32\,K\,\delta^{1/2} = \tfrac32\,F/\delta = \tfrac32\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\), because the derivative of the power is \(\tfrac32\,K\,\delta^{1/2}\). For the bearing of section 25.9 the static load is \(283{,}7\) N, the tangent stiffness \(8{,}538 \cdot 10^7\) N/m and the approach \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = 4{,}98\) µm. If we divided the force by the tangent stiffness we would get \(283{,}7/(8{,}538 \cdot 10^7)\) m \(= 3{,}32\) µm, by the secant \(4{,}98\) µm. The ratio \(k_{\mathrm{t}}/k_{\mathrm{s}}\) is \(1{,}499\), which is \(3/2\) up to rounding. A spring with one stiffness must therefore use the secant in statics and the tangent in vibration.

The law \(F = K\,\delta^{3/2}\) also allows a computation of impact.

From history

Hertz presented the solution of the compression of two elastic bodies to the Physical Society in Berlin in January 1881, applied it to special cases and extended it to impact, for which he derived formulas for the duration of the impact of two spheres and for the stresses during it (TIMO, PDF p. 287).

The computation of impact thus follows from the force law: the force is a known function of the approach, so we insert it into Newton's law. In LOVE this is equation (61), \(P = k\,\alpha^{3/2}\), where \(k\) and \(\alpha\) mean our \(K\) and \(\delta\) (LOVE, PDF p. 218). It holds only if the duration of the impact is a large multiple of the longest natural period of vibration of either body, because only then does the compression at the contact behave as a static phenomenon (LOVE, PDF pp. 217-218). Here we show only what we get when this is satisfied. We send a ball of mass \(m\) with speed \(v\) against a flat body that we take to be at rest. This is an idealization: for a movable body the reduced mass of both bodies would appear in place of \(m\) (LOVE, PDF p. 218). At time \(t = 0\) they touch and \(m\,\ddot\delta = -K\,\delta^{3/2}\) holds. We multiply the equation by \(\dot\delta\), write both sides as a derivative, \(\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(\tfrac12\,m\,\dot\delta^2\big) = -\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(\tfrac25\,K\,\delta^{5/2}\big)\), and integrate from \(t = 0\), where \(\delta = 0\) and \(\dot\delta = v\):

\[\tfrac12\,m\,\dot\delta^2 + \tfrac25\,K\,\delta^{5/2} = \tfrac12\,m\,v^2 . \tag{25.48}\]

At the largest approach \(\dot\delta = 0\), so \(\delta_{\max} = \big(5\,m\,v^2/(4K)\big)^{2/5}\). From (25.48) it follows that \(\dot\delta = v\sqrt{1 - (\delta/\delta_{\max})^{5/2}}\). During the approach \(\dot\delta > 0\), so \(\delta\) is an increasing function of time and has an inverse function \(t(\delta)\) with the derivative \(1/\dot\delta\). The time of approach is therefore \(\int_0^{\delta_{\max}} \frac{1}{\dot\delta}\,\mathrm{d}\delta\), and with the substitution \(x = \delta/\delta_{\max}\) it is \(\frac{\delta_{\max}}{v}\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{5/2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The rebound is the approach reversed, because the force is a function of \(\delta\) only, so the duration of the impact is twice the time of approach:

\[T = \frac{2\,\delta_{\max}}{v}\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{5/2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{25.49}\]

The integral is improper, because the integrand is unbounded at \(x = 1\). We understand it as the limit of the integrals from \(0\) to \(1 - h\) as \(h > 0\) goes to \(0\), just as definition 9.16 takes the limit of the integrals up to \(T\). Since \(x^{5/2} \le x\) on \([0, 1]\), the positive integrand is at most \(1/\sqrt{1 - x}\), whose integral from \(0\) to \(1 - h\) is \(2 - 2\sqrt h < 2\). The integrals up to \(1 - h\) therefore grow as \(h\) decreases and are bounded by \(2\), so they have a limit (the proof is the same as for theorem 1.51). Its value is \(1{,}4716\) (NumPy, num-10.py). Take a steel ball of diameter \(12{,}7\) mm and density \(7800\) kg/m³, so \(m = 8{,}37\) g, hitting a steel flat body with speed \(1\) m/s, which is the speed after a fall from a height of \(51\) mm. We get \(\delta_{\max} = 15{,}29\) µm, \(F_{\max} = 684\) N and \(T = 45{,}0\) µs. The contact radius is then \(a = 311{,}6\) µm and \(a/R = 0{,}049\), so much smaller than the radius of the ball, as the idealization of a non-conforming contact requires (section 25.5). For the period of vibration of the ball the book has no expression. As an estimate of the order of magnitude we take the time that a wave along a rod with speed \(c = \sqrt{E/\rho} = 5013\) m/s (lemma 13.26) needs to cross the diameter, \(D/c = 2{,}53\) µs. The duration \(T\) is \(17{,}8\) times longer, so the condition from LOVE is satisfied with a large margin, if this estimate is really a measure of the period, which the book does not prove. The largest pressure \(p_0 = 3364\) MPa is beyond the elastic limit of mild steel (section 25.6), so the computation holds for the hardened steel of bearings and not for the steel of the book.

  • The half-space and contact in FEM: the solutions of Flamant (theorem 25.13) and Boussinesq (theorem 25.15) were promised in chapter 11. By corollary 25.16 the displacement of the half-space falls only as \(1/r\), so a truncated body in a finite element model loses part of the displacement that the half-space has far from the contact. How much, the book does not compute (AK, chapter 15). The displacement under a point force is infinite, also for a plane body, where chapter 17 shows it by energy (AK). Contact in finite elements needs elements that look for the gap and the pressure by the conditions 25.19, and these are outside this chapter (AK, chapter 15). The uniqueness of the contact problem itself, which chapter 11 left to this chapter, is not proved here either. The reason is that the contact conditions are inequalities and the contact area is an unknown.
  • The bearing in a rotor model: the tangent stiffness matrix of the bearing \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) of theorem 25.40 is added into the diagonal of the system like a spring, as in theorem 7.13, and the natural frequencies are by theorem 10.2 and theorem 10.13 the eigenvalues of the corresponding problem. Chapter 24 (DSK) adds the rotation of the shaft with gyroscopic terms and critical speeds, where the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) enters as data. Our two bearings have no speed terms (centrifugal forces and the gyroscopic effect neglected, section 25.7).
  • Bearing damping: FPGL states that damping in rolling bearings is small and that the coefficient \(c\) is typically \((0{,}25 \text{ to } 2{,}5) \cdot 10^{-5}\) s times a typical stiffness \(k\) of the bearing (FPGL, PDF p. 203). For the stiffness \(8{,}538 \cdot 10^7\) N/m of our bearing this gives \(213\) to \(2134\) N s/m, but this is a datum of the source and not our computation. Chapter 20 (DSK) shows how \(c\) enters the equations of motion.
  • Limits of the chapter: the idealizations are named in the sections. The Winkler foundation is a force per length with no coupling between points, the half-space is linearly elastic, isotropic and frictionless, the Hertz contact is non-conforming and frictionless, the bearing has rigid rings, is at rest and is not loaded by speed forces. Elastohydrodynamic lubrication, friction and shear on the contact surface, crowning and edge loading of rollers, service life and combined axial loads are only named by the chapter. Stated without proof are: the quadratic form of the Hertz displacement away from the centre (from the sources and checked numerically), the elliptic contact, the uniqueness of the half-space and of contact problems, Palmgren's formula for \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the law \(n = 10/9\) for rollers (both empirical), the convergence of Newton's iteration for systems and the stiffness ratios of Kramer.
